mcqs.why: The lines meet where 5x + 4y = 120 and x + 2y = 36: twice the second subtracted from the first gives 3x = 48, so x = 16, y = 10. Evaluate P: (0, 0) gives 0; (24, 0) gives 960; (16, 10) gives 40(16) + 50(10) = 640 + 500 = 1140; (0, 18) gives 900. Maximum is Rs. 1140.

mcqs.q: A company makes lamps L₁ (x) and L₂ (y) with 2x + y ≤ 40 and x + y ≤ 32, profit P = 70x + 50y. The maximum profit is:
mcqs.why: Subtract x + y = 32 from 2x + y = 40: x = 8, then y = 24. Evaluate P: (0, 0) gives 0; (20, 0) gives 1400; (8, 24) gives 70(8) + 50(24) = 560 + 1200 = 1760; (0, 32) gives 1600. Maximum is Rs. 1760 at (8, 24).

lessons.title: Review Exercise 9
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The feasible triangle for 0 ≤ x ≤ 5 with 0 ≤ y ≤ x has vertices (0, 0), (5, 0) and (5, 5).
  • A profit function taking values 11 at (3, 7) and 7 at (1, 3) is P = −8x + 5y: −24 + 35 = 11 and −8 + 15 = 7.
  • For f = 7x + 11y at (6, 2), (4, 6), (5, 4), (3, 6) the values are 64, 94, 79, 87, so the maximum is 94.
  • The point (3, −2) satisfies both 2x + 3y ≤ 6 and 3x − 2y ≤ 16, while the other listed points each fail one constraint.
  • f = 5x + 3y with only x ≥ 3, y ≥ 3 has no maximum, because the region is unbounded.
  • Maximize 5x + 7y under 2x + 3y ≤ 12, x + y ≤ 5, x, y ≥ 0 gives maximum 29 at (3, 2).
  • Z = 4x + 3y under 3x + 4y ≤ 24, 8x + 6y ≤ 48, x ≤ 5, y ≤ 6, x, y ≥ 0 has maximum 24, attained at both (5, (4)/(3)) and ((24)/(7), (24)/(7)).
  • Diet problem: least cost is Rs. 112 at 2 kg of food X and 4 kg of food Y, from C = 16x + 20y at the corners (10, 0), (2, 4), (1, 5), (0, 8).

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Choose the correct option: The solution of the system x ≥ 0, x − 5 ≤ 0 and x ≥ y is a polygonal region, whose vertices are:

Options: (a) (0, 0), (5, 0), (5, 5) (b) (0, 0), (0, 5), (5, 5) (c) (5, 5), (0, 5), (5, 0) (d) (0, 0), (0, 5), (5, 0)

Correct answer: (0, 0), (5, 0), (5, 5)

Q: Q1(ii). Choose the correct option: Find the profit function p if it yields the value 11 and 7 at (3, 7) and (1, 3) respectively.

Options: (a) P = −8x + 5y (b) p = 8x − 5y (c) p = 8x + 5y (d) p = −(8x + 5y)

Correct answer: P = −8x + 5y

Q: Q1(iii). Choose the correct option: The vertices of closed convex polygon of the feasible region are (6, 2), (4, 6), (5, 4) and (3, 6). The maximum value of the objective function f = 7x + 11y is:

Options: (a) 64 (b) 79 (c) 94 (d) 87

Correct answer: 94

Q: Q1(iv). Choose the correct option: Which of the following point is in the feasible region determined by the inequalities 2x + 3y ≤ 6 and 3x − 2y ≤ 16?

Options: (a) (4, −3) (b) (−2, 4) (c) (3, −2) (d) (3, −4)

Correct answer: (3, −2)

Q: Q1(v). Choose the correct option: The maximum value of f = 5x + 3y subject to the constraints x ≥ 3 and y ≥ 3 is ______.

Options: (a) 15 (b) 9 (c) 24 (d) does not exist

Correct answer: does not exist

Q: Q1(vi). Choose the correct option: Maximize 5x + 7y subject to 2x + 3y ≤ 12, x + y ≤ 5, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

Options: (a) 29 (b) 30 (c) 28 (d) 31

Correct answer: 29

Q: Q2. Maximize Z = 4x + 3y subject to the constraints 3x + 4y ≤ 24, 8x + 6y ≤ 48, x ≤ 5, y ≤ 6, x, y ≥ 0.

Ans: Formula: Corner-point method: evaluate Z at every corner point of the feasible region; the largest value is the maximum
Step 1: Line 1: 3x + 4y = 24. Intercepts: (8, 0) and (0, 6). Shade the origin side.
Step 2: Line 2: 8x + 6y = 48. Intercepts: (6, 0) and (0, 8). Shade the origin side.
Step 3: x ≤ 5 is the region left of the vertical line x = 5; y ≤ 6 is the region below the horizontal line y = 6; x, y ≥ 0 give the first quadrant.
Step 4: Corner points: (0, 0); (5, 0) where x = 5 meets the x-axis; where x = 5 meets line 2: 8(5) + 6y = 48 gives y = (4)/(3), corner (5, (4)/(3)) (it satisfies line 1: 15 + (16)/(3) = (61)/(3) ≤ 24 ✓; the meeting of x = 5 with line 1, (5, (9)/(4)), fails line 2 and is not feasible); intersection of lines 1 and 2: solving 3x + 4y = 24 and 8x + 6y = 48 gives x = (24)/(7), y = (24)/(7), corner ((24)/(7), (24)/(7)) (it satisfies x ≤ 5 and y ≤ 6 ✓); on the y-axis line 1 gives (0, 6), which also lies on y = 6 and satisfies line 2 (36 ≤ 48 ✓).
Step 5: Evaluate Z = 4x + 3y at each corner:
At (0, 0): Z = 0.
At (5, 0): Z = 4(5) + 3(0) = 20.
At (5, (4)/(3)): Z = 4(5) + 3((4)/(3)) = 20 + 4 = 24.
At ((24)/(7), (24)/(7)): Z = 4((24)/(7)) + 3((24)/(7)) = (96)/(7) + (72)/(7) = (168)/(7) = 24.
At (0, 6): Z = 4(0) + 3(6) = 18.
Step 6: The largest value is 24, attained at two corners (5, (4)/(3)) and ((24)/(7), (24)/(7)); since Z = 4x + 3y is parallel to the side 8x + 6y = 48 joining them, Z = 24 at every point of that side as well.
Answer: The maximum value of Z is 24, attained at (5, (4)/(3)) and at ((24)/(7), (24)/(7)) (and at every point of the segment joining them)
Graph (in words): Draw the x and y axes and work in the first quadrant. Draw solid lines for 3x + 4y = 24 (through (8, 0) and (0, 6)), 8x + 6y = 48 (through (6, 0) and (0, 8)), the vertical line x = 5 and the horizontal line y = 6. Shade the pentagon with labelled corners (0, 0), (5, 0), (5, (4)/(3)), ((24)/(7), (24)/(7)) and (0, 6). The maximum Z = 24 is marked along the whole side between (5, (4)/(3)) and ((24)/(7), (24)/(7)).

Q: Q3. A dietician wishes to mix two type of foods in such a way that the vitamin content of the mixture contains at least 10 units of vitamin A, at least 12 units of vitamin B and at least 8 units of vitamin C. The vitamin content per kg of each food is given in the table: Food X contains vitamin A 1 unit, vitamin B 2 units, vitamin C 3 units per kg; Food Y contains vitamin A 2 units, vitamin B 2 units, vitamin C 1 unit per kg. Food X costs Rs. 16 per kg and food Y costs Rs. 20 per kg. Find the least cost of the mixture which will produce the required diet.

Ans: Formula: Corner-point method for minimization: model with variables, graph the feasible region (here unbounded), evaluate the cost at every corner; the smallest value is the least cost
Step 1: Let x = kg of food X and y = kg of food Y in the mixture.
Step 2: Vitamin A: x + 2y ≥ 10. Vitamin B: 2x + 2y ≥ 12, i.e. x + y ≥ 6. Vitamin C: 3x + y ≥ 8. Also x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
Step 3: Cost function: C = 16x + 20y (to be minimized).
Step 4: Boundary lines: x + 2y = 10 through (10, 0) and (0, 5); x + y = 6 through (6, 0) and (0, 6); 3x + y = 8 through ((8)/(3), 0) and (0, 8). For each, shade the side away from the origin.
Step 5: Corner points: on the x-axis, x + 2y = 10 gives (10, 0) (check: 10 ≥ 6 ✓, 30 ≥ 8 ✓); intersection of x + 2y = 10 and x + y = 6: subtract, y = 4, then x = 2, corner (2, 4) (check: 3(2) + 4 = 10 ≥ 8 ✓); intersection of x + y = 6 and 3x + y = 8: subtract, 2x = 2, so x = 1, y = 5, corner (1, 5) (check: 1 + 10 = 11 ≥ 10 ✓); on the y-axis, 3x + y = 8 gives (0, 8) (check: 16 ≥ 10 ✓, 8 ≥ 6 ✓).
Step 6: Evaluate C = 16x + 20y at each corner:
At (10, 0): C = 16(10) + 20(0) = 160.
At (2, 4): C = 16(2) + 20(4) = 32 + 80 = 112.
At (1, 5): C = 16(1) + 20(5) = 16 + 100 = 116.
At (0, 8): C = 16(0) + 20(8) = 160.
Step 7: The smallest cost is Rs. 112 at (2, 4).
Answer: The least cost is Rs. 112, using 2 kg of food X and 4 kg of food Y
Graph (in words): Draw the x-axis (kg of food X) and y-axis (kg of food Y) and work in the first quadrant. Draw solid lines for x + 2y = 10 (through (10, 0) and (0, 5)), x + y = 6 (through (6, 0) and (0, 6)) and 3x + y = 8 (through ((8)/(3), 0) and (0, 8)). Shade the unbounded region above all three lines, whose boundary runs from (10, 0) up-left along x + 2y = 10 to the corner (2, 4), then along x + y = 6 to the corner (1, 5), then along 3x + y = 8 up to (0, 8), and then up the y-axis. The least cost Rs. 112 is marked at the corner (2, 4).

Q: Q4. Find maximum and minimum values of Z = 5x + 10y subject to constraints x + 2y > 120, x + y > 60, x − 2y > 0, x, y > 0.

Ans: Formula: Corner-point method: the objective is bounded only if the feasible region is bounded in the relevant direction; here the region is unbounded above
Step 1: Boundary line 1: x + 2y = 120. Intercepts: (120, 0) and (0, 60). The feasible side is the side away from the origin (0 > 120 is false).
Step 2: Boundary line 2: x + y = 60. Intercepts: (60, 0) and (0, 60). Feasible side away from the origin; this line does not cut the region further, since on x + 2y > 120 with y > 0 we already have x + y > 60 wherever the third condition also holds near the corner found below.
Step 3: Boundary line 3: x − 2y = 0, i.e. x = 2y, a line through the origin; the feasible side is x > 2y.
Step 4: Corner of the (closed) boundary: solve x + 2y = 120 with x = 2y: 2y + 2y = 120, so y = 30 and x = 60. Point (60, 30). Check line 2: 60 + 30 = 90 > 60 ✓.
Step 5: Value of Z at (60, 30): Z = 5(60) + 10(30) = 300 + 300 = 600. Note Z = 5(x + 2y), so on the whole boundary segment x + 2y = 120 (from (60, 30) towards (120, 0)) Z = 600, and inside the region Z > 600.
Step 6: The region is unbounded: for example points (3t, t) with t large satisfy all the constraints, and Z = 5(3t) + 10(t) = 25t grows without limit. So Z has no maximum value.
Step 7: Because the printed inequalities are strict (>), the boundary itself is excluded, so the value 600 is approached but not attained; it is the greatest lower bound (infimum) of Z, attained at (60, 30) if the boundary is included.
Answer: Z has no maximum value (the feasible region is unbounded); the minimum (boundary) value of Z is 600 at (60, 30), not attained for the strict inequalities as printed
Note: The book's printed answer calls 600 the maximum value of Z at (120, 0) and (60, 30); this is incorrect — 600 is the minimum (boundary) value, and Z has no maximum because the feasible region is unbounded.
Graph (in words): Draw the x and y axes. Draw the line x + 2y = 120 through (120, 0) and (0, 60), the line x + y = 60 through (60, 0) and (0, 60) (it lies below the shaded region), and the line x = 2y through the origin and (60, 30). The feasible region is the open wedge above the line x + 2y = 120 and to the right of the line x = 2y, with its corner at (60, 30); it opens out indefinitely upwards and to the right, which is why Z increases without limit. Since the inequalities are strict, the boundary lines are drawn dashed.

mcqs.q: The solution of the system x ≥ 0, x − 5 ≤ 0 and x ≥ y (with y ≥ 0) is a polygonal region, whose vertices are:
mcqs.why: The conditions give 0 ≤ x ≤ 5 and 0 ≤ y ≤ x. At x = 0 only y = 0 is allowed, giving (0, 0); at x = 5, y ranges from 0 to 5, giving (5, 0) and (5, 5). These three points are the vertices of the triangular region.

The vertices of the closed convex polygon of the feasible region are (6, 2), (4, 6), (5, 4) and (3, 6). The maximum value of f = 7x + 11y is:
Which of the following points is in the feasible region determined by 2x + 3y ≤ 6 and 3x − 2y ≤ 16?
mcqs.why: Test (3, −2): 2(3) + 3(−2) = 0 ≤ 6 ✓ and 3(3) − 2(−2) = 13 ≤ 16 ✓. The others fail: (4, −3) gives 18 > 16 in the second, (−2, 4) gives 8 > 6 in the first, (3, −4) gives 17 > 16 in the second.

mcqs.q: The maximum value of f = 5x + 3y subject to the constraints x ≥ 3 and y ≥ 3 is ______.
mcqs.why: The constraints x ≥ 3 and y ≥ 3 leave x and y free to grow without bound, so f = 5x + 3y also grows without bound. Hence no maximum value exists.

mcqs.q: Maximize 5x + 7y subject to 2x + 3y ≤ 12, x + y ≤ 5, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
mcqs.why: Corners: (0, 0) gives 0; (5, 0) gives 25; (0, 4) gives 28; the lines meet where 2x + 3y = 12 and x + y = 5: subtracting twice the second from the first gives y = 2, x = 3, and 5(3) + 7(2) = 15 + 14 = 29. The maximum is 29.

mcqs.q: For Z = 4x + 3y under 3x + 4y ≤ 24, 8x + 6y ≤ 48, x ≤ 5, y ≤ 6, x, y ≥ 0, the maximum value of Z is:
In the diet problem (cost C = 16x + 20y, corners (10, 0), (2, 4), (1, 5), (0, 8)), the least cost is:
In the diet problem, the vitamin constraints for x kg of food X and y kg of food Y are:
mcqs.why: Vitamin A: X gives 1 and Y gives 2 per kg, need at least 10: x + 2y ≥ 10. Vitamin B: 2x + 2y ≥ 12 simplifies to x + y ≥ 6. Vitamin C: X gives 3 and Y gives 1, need at least 8: 3x + y ≥ 8.

mcqs.q: For Z = 5x + 10y subject to x + 2y > 120, x + y > 60, x − 2y > 0, x, y > 0, the correct statement is:
options: No maximum; 600 is the boundary minimum value at (60, 30)
mcqs.why: Solve x + 2y = 120 with x = 2y: 4y = 120, so y = 30, x = 60, and Z = 5(60) + 10(30) = 600 there. But the region is unbounded: points (3t, t) are feasible for large t and give Z = 25t, which grows without limit. So Z has no maximum; 600 is its lower boundary value. The book wrongly calls 600 the maximum.

chapters.title: Unit 10: Trigonometric Identities of Sum and Difference of Angles

lessons.title: Exercise 10.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • sin37° cos22° + cos37° sin22° = sin59° by sin(α + β); cos83° cos53° + sin83° sin53° = cos30° by cos(α − β).
  • cos19° cos5° − sin19° sin5° = cos24°; sin40° cos15° − cos40° sin15° = sin25°.
  • (tan20° + tan32°)/(1 − tan20° tan32°) = tan52° and (tan35° − tan12°)/(1 + tan35° tan12°) = tan23°.
  • sin(π/12) = sin15° = (√6 − √2)/(4) and cos15° = (√6 + √2)/(4), from 15° = 45° − 30°.
  • tan75° = 2 + √3 and tan105° = −2 − √3, from the tan(α + β) identity.
  • With sin u = (3)/(5), sin v = (4)/(5) in Quadrant I: cos(u + v) = 0, sin(u − v) = −(7)/(25), cos(u − v) = (24)/(25), tan(u − v) = −(7)/(24).
  • With sin α = −(4)/(5) (Quadrant III) and cos β = −(12)/(13) (Quadrant II): sin(α − β) = (63)/(65), cos(α + β) = (56)/(65), tan(α + β) = (33)/(56).
  • 4sinθ + 3cosθ = 5 sin(θ + φ) with cos φ = (4)/(5), sin φ = (3)/(5); 15sinθ + 8cosθ has r = 17; sinθ + cosθ = √2 sin(θ + 45°).

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Write as a trigonometric function of a single angle: sin37° cos22° + cos37° sin22°

Ans: Identity used: sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β
The given expression has exactly the form of the right hand side of this identity, with α = 37° and β = 22°.
So sin37° cos22° + cos37° sin22° = sin(37° + 22°)
= sin59°
Answer: sin59°

Q: Q1(ii). Write as a trigonometric function of a single angle: cos83° cos53° + sin83° sin53°

Ans: Identity used: cos(α − β) = cos α cos β + sin α sin β
The given expression has exactly the form of the right hand side of this identity, with α = 83° and β = 53°.
So cos83° cos53° + sin83° sin53° = cos(83° − 53°)
= cos30°
Answer: cos30°

Q: Q1(iii). Write as a trigonometric function of a single angle: cos19° cos5° − sin19° sin5°

Ans: Identity used: cos(α + β) = cos α cos β − sin α sin β
The given expression has exactly the form of the right hand side of this identity, with α = 19° and β = 5°.
So cos19° cos5° − sin19° sin5° = cos(19° + 5°)
= cos24°
Answer: cos24°

Q: Q1(iv). Write as a trigonometric function of a single angle: sin40° cos15° − cos40° sin15°

Ans: Identity used: sin(α − β) = sin α cos β − cos α sin β
The given expression has exactly the form of the right hand side of this identity, with α = 40° and β = 15°.
So sin40° cos15° − cos40° sin15° = sin(40° − 15°)
= sin25°
Answer: sin25°

Q: Q1(v). Write as a trigonometric function of a single angle: (tan20° + tan32°)/(1 − tan20° tan32°)

Ans: Identity used: tan(α + β) = (tan α + tan β)/(1 − tan α tan β)
The given expression has exactly the form of the right hand side of this identity, with α = 20° and β = 32°.
So (tan20° + tan32°)/(1 − tan20° tan32°) = tan(20° + 32°)
= tan52°
Answer: tan52°

Q: Q1(vi). Write as a trigonometric function of a single angle: (tan35° − tan12°)/(1 + tan35° tan12°)

Ans: Identity used: tan(α − β) = (tan α − tan β)/(1 + tan α tan β)
The given expression has exactly the form of the right hand side of this identity, with α = 35° and β = 12°.
So (tan35° − tan12°)/(1 + tan35° tan12°) = tan(35° − 12°)
= tan23°
Answer: tan23°

Q: Q2(i). Evaluate exactly: sin(π/12)

Ans: Method: write (π)/(12) = 15° as a difference of known angles, 45° − 30°, and use sin(α − β) = sin α cos β − cos α sin β.
sin(π/12) = sin15°
= sin(45° − 30°)
= sin45° cos30° − cos45° sin30° [by sin(α − β) identity]
= ((√2)/(2))((√3)/(2)) − ((√2)/(2))((1)/(2))
= (√6)/(4) − (√2)/(4)
= (√6 − √2)/(4)
Answer: (√6 − √2)/(4)

Q: Q2(ii). Evaluate exactly: tan75°

Ans: Method: write 75° = 45° + 30° and use tan(α + β) = (tan α + tan β)/(1 − tan α tan β).
tan75° = tan(45° + 30°)
= (tan45° + tan30°)/(1 − tan45° tan30°)
= (1 + (1)/(√3))/(1 − (1)/(√3))
= (√3 + 1)/(√3 − 1)
Rationalising the denominator, multiply numerator and denominator by (√3 + 1):
= ((√3 + 1)²)/((√3)² − 1²)
= (3 + 2√3 + 1)/(3 − 1)
= (4 + 2√3)/(2)
= 2 + √3
Answer: 2 + √3

Q: Q2(iii). Evaluate exactly: tan105°

Ans: Method: write 105° = 60° + 45° and use tan(α + β) = (tan α + tan β)/(1 − tan α tan β).
tan105° = tan(60° + 45°)
= (tan60° + tan45°)/(1 − tan60° tan45°)
= (√3 + 1)/(1 − √3)
Rationalising the denominator, multiply numerator and denominator by (1 + √3):
= ((√3 + 1)(1 + √3))/((1 − √3)(1 + √3))
= (4 + 2√3)/(1 − 3)
= (4 + 2√3)/(−2)
= −2 − √3
Answer: −2 − √3

Q: Q2(iv). Evaluate exactly: tan(5π/12)

Ans: Method: (5π)/(12) = 75°, and 75° = 45° + 30°, so use tan(α + β) = (tan α + tan β)/(1 − tan α tan β).
tan(5π/12) = tan75°
= tan(45° + 30°)
= (tan45° + tan30°)/(1 − tan45° tan30°)
= (1 + (1)/(√3))/(1 − (1)/(√3))
= (√3 + 1)/(√3 − 1)
= ((√3 + 1)²)/((√3)² − 1²) [rationalising]
= (4 + 2√3)/(2)
= 2 + √3
Answer: 2 + √3

Q: Q2(v). Evaluate exactly: cos15°

Ans: Method: write 15° = 45° − 30° and use cos(α − β) = cos α cos β + sin α sin β.
cos15° = cos(45° − 30°)
= cos45° cos30° + sin45° sin30° [by cos(α − β) identity]
= ((√2)/(2))((√3)/(2)) + ((√2)/(2))((1)/(2))
= (√6)/(4) + (√2)/(4)
= (√6 + √2)/(4)
Answer: (√6 + √2)/(4)

Q: Q2(vi). Evaluate exactly: sin(7π/12)

Ans: Method: (7π)/(12) = 105° = 60° + 45°, so use sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β.
sin(7π/12) = sin105°
= sin(60° + 45°)
= sin60° cos45° + cos60° sin45° [by sin(α + β) identity]
= ((√3)/(2))((√2)/(2)) + ((1)/(2))((√2)/(2))
= (√6)/(4) + (√2)/(4)
= (√6 + √2)/(4)
Answer: (√6 + √2)/(4)

Q: Q3(i). If sin u = (3)/(5) and sin v = (4)/(5), where u and v are between 0 and (π)/(2), evaluate exactly: cos(u + v)

Ans: First find cos u and cos v. Since u and v are in the first quadrant, their cosines are positive.
Identity used: sin²x + cos²x = 1
cos²u = 1 − sin²u = 1 − (9)/(25) = (16)/(25), so cos u = (4)/(5)
cos²v = 1 − sin²v = 1 − (16)/(25) = (9)/(25), so cos v = (3)/(5)
Identity used: cos(u + v) = cos u cos v − sin u sin v
cos(u + v) = ((4)/(5))((3)/(5)) − ((3)/(5))((4)/(5))
= (12)/(25) − (12)/(25)
= 0
Answer: 0

Q: Q3(ii). If sin u = (3)/(5) and sin v = (4)/(5), where u and v are between 0 and (π)/(2), evaluate exactly: tan(u − v)

Ans: First find cos u and cos v. Since u and v are in the first quadrant, their cosines are positive.
Identity used: sin²x + cos²x = 1
cos²u = 1 − (9)/(25) = (16)/(25), so cos u = (4)/(5) and tan u = (sin u)/(cos u) = (3)/(4)
cos²v = 1 − (16)/(25) = (9)/(25), so cos v = (3)/(5) and tan v = (sin v)/(cos v) = (4)/(3)
Identity used: tan(u − v) = (tan u − tan v)/(1 + tan u tan v)
tan(u − v) = ((3)/(4) − (4)/(3))/(1 + ((3)/(4))((4)/(3)))
= (−(7)/(12))/(1 + 1)
= (−(7)/(12))/(2)
= −(7)/(24)
Answer: −(7)/(24)

Q: Q3(iii). If sin u = (3)/(5) and sin v = (4)/(5), where u and v are between 0 and (π)/(2), evaluate exactly: sin(u − v)

Ans: First find cos u and cos v. Since u and v are in the first quadrant, their cosines are positive.
Identity used: sin²x + cos²x = 1
cos²u = 1 − (9)/(25) = (16)/(25), so cos u = (4)/(5)
cos²v = 1 − (16)/(25) = (9)/(25), so cos v = (3)/(5)
Identity used: sin(u − v) = sin u cos v − cos u sin v
sin(u − v) = ((3)/(5))((3)/(5)) − ((4)/(5))((4)/(5))
= (9)/(25) − (16)/(25)
= −(7)/(25)
Answer: −(7)/(25)

Q: Q3(iv). If sin u = (3)/(5) and sin v = (4)/(5), where u and v are between 0 and (π)/(2), evaluate exactly: cos(u − v)

Ans: First find cos u and cos v. Since u and v are in the first quadrant, their cosines are positive.
Identity used: sin²x + cos²x = 1
cos²u = 1 − (9)/(25) = (16)/(25), so cos u = (4)/(5)
cos²v = 1 − (16)/(25) = (9)/(25), so cos v = (3)/(5)
Identity used: cos(u − v) = cos u cos v + sin u sin v
cos(u − v) = ((4)/(5))((3)/(5)) + ((3)/(5))((4)/(5))
= (12)/(25) + (12)/(25)
= (24)/(25)
Answer: (24)/(25)

Q: Q4(i). If sin α = −(4)/(5) and cos β = −(12)/(13), with α in Quadrant III and β in Quadrant II, find the exact value of: sin(α − β)

Ans: First find cos α and sin β using sin²x + cos²x = 1, taking signs from the quadrants.
cos²α = 1 − sin²α = 1 − (16)/(25) = (9)/(25); α is in Quadrant III, where cosine is negative, so cos α = −(3)/(5)
sin²β = 1 − cos²β = 1 − (144)/(169) = (25)/(169); β is in Quadrant II, where sine is positive, so sin β = (5)/(13)
Identity used: sin(α − β) = sin α cos β − cos α sin β
sin(α − β) = (−(4)/(5))(−(12)/(13)) − (−(3)/(5))((5)/(13))
= (48)/(65) + (15)/(65)
= (63)/(65)
Answer: (63)/(65)

Q: Q4(ii). If sin α = −(4)/(5) and cos β = −(12)/(13), with α in Quadrant III and β in Quadrant II, find the exact value of: cos(α + β)

Ans: First find cos α and sin β using sin²x + cos²x = 1, taking signs from the quadrants.
cos²α = 1 − (16)/(25) = (9)/(25); α is in Quadrant III, so cos α = −(3)/(5)
sin²β = 1 − (144)/(169) = (25)/(169); β is in Quadrant II, so sin β = (5)/(13)
Identity used: cos(α + β) = cos α cos β − sin α sin β
cos(α + β) = (−(3)/(5))(−(12)/(13)) − (−(4)/(5))((5)/(13))
= (36)/(65) + (20)/(65)
= (56)/(65)
Answer: (56)/(65)

Q: Q4(iii). If sin α = −(4)/(5) and cos β = −(12)/(13), with α in Quadrant III and β in Quadrant II, find the exact value of: tan(α + β)

Ans: First find cos α and sin β using sin²x + cos²x = 1, taking signs from the quadrants.
cos²α = 1 − (16)/(25) = (9)/(25); α is in Quadrant III, so cos α = −(3)/(5)
sin²β = 1 − (144)/(169) = (25)/(169); β is in Quadrant II, so sin β = (5)/(13)
Identity used: sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β
sin(α + β) = (−(4)/(5))(−(12)/(13)) + (−(3)/(5))((5)/(13)) = (48)/(65) − (15)/(65) = (33)/(65)
Identity used: cos(α + β) = cos α cos β − sin α sin β
cos(α + β) = (−(3)/(5))(−(12)/(13)) − (−(4)/(5))((5)/(13)) = (36)/(65) + (20)/(65) = (56)/(65)
Now tan(α + β) = (sin(α + β))/(cos(α + β))
= ((33)/(65))/((56)/(65))
= (33)/(56)
Answer: (33)/(56)

Q: Q5(i). If tan α = (3)/(4) and sec β = (13)/(5), and neither the terminal side of α nor of β is in the first quadrant, find: sin(α + β)

Ans: First fix the quadrants and find sin α, cos α, sin β, cos β.
tan α = (3)/(4) is positive but α is not in Quadrant I, so α is in Quadrant III; hence sin α and cos α are both negative.
For α: opposite = 3, adjacent = 4, hypotenuse = √(3² + 4²) = 5, so sin α = −(3)/(5) and cos α = −(4)/(5)
sec β = (13)/(5) gives cos β = (5)/(13), which is positive; β is not in Quadrant I, so β is in Quadrant IV, where sine is negative.
sin²β = 1 − cos²β = 1 − (25)/(169) = (144)/(169), so sin β = −(12)/(13)
Identity used: sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β
sin(α + β) = (−(3)/(5))((5)/(13)) + (−(4)/(5))(−(12)/(13))
= −(15)/(65) + (48)/(65)
= (33)/(65)
Answer: (33)/(65)

Q: Q5(ii). If tan α = (3)/(4) and sec β = (13)/(5), and neither the terminal side of α nor of β is in the first quadrant, find: cos(α + β)

Ans: First fix the quadrants and find sin α, cos α, sin β, cos β.
tan α = (3)/(4) is positive but α is not in Quadrant I, so α is in Quadrant III: sin α = −(3)/(5), cos α = −(4)/(5) (hypotenuse √(3² + 4²) = 5)
sec β = (13)/(5) gives cos β = (5)/(13) > 0; β is not in Quadrant I, so β is in Quadrant IV: sin β = −(12)/(13) (from sin²β = 1 − (25)/(169) = (144)/(169))
Identity used: cos(α + β) = cos α cos β − sin α sin β
cos(α + β) = (−(4)/(5))((5)/(13)) − (−(3)/(5))(−(12)/(13))
= −(20)/(65) − (36)/(65)
= −(56)/(65)
Answer: −(56)/(65)

Q: Q5(iii). If tan α = (3)/(4) and sec β = (13)/(5), and neither the terminal side of α nor of β is in the first quadrant, find: tan(α + β)

Ans: First fix the quadrants and find the needed ratios.
α is in Quadrant III (tan α > 0, not Quadrant I): sin α = −(3)/(5), cos α = −(4)/(5)
β is in Quadrant IV (cos β = (5)/(13) > 0, not Quadrant I): sin β = −(12)/(13)
Identity used: sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β
sin(α + β) = (−(3)/(5))((5)/(13)) + (−(4)/(5))(−(12)/(13)) = −(15)/(65) + (48)/(65) = (33)/(65)
Identity used: cos(α + β) = cos α cos β − sin α sin β
cos(α + β) = (−(4)/(5))((5)/(13)) − (−(3)/(5))(−(12)/(13)) = −(20)/(65) − (36)/(65) = −(56)/(65)
Now tan(α + β) = (sin(α + β))/(cos(α + β)) = ((33)/(65))/(−(56)/(65))
= −(33)/(56)
Answer: −(33)/(56)

Q: Q6(i). Show that: cos α = 2cos²(α/2) − 1 = 1 − 2sin²(α/2)

Ans: Identity used: the double-angle identities cos2x = 2cos²x − 1 and cos2x = 1 − 2sin²x, with x = (α)/(2).
Put x = (α)/(2), so that 2x = α.
Then cos α = cos(2x) [replacing α by 2x]
= 2cos²x − 1 [by cos2x = 2cos²x − 1]
= 2cos²(α/2) − 1 [putting x = (α)/(2) back]
Also cos α = cos(2x)
= 1 − 2sin²x [by cos2x = 1 − 2sin²x]
= 1 − 2sin²(α/2)
Hence cos α = 2cos²(α/2) − 1 = 1 − 2sin²(α/2).
Hence proved.

Q: Q6(ii). Show that: sin(α + β) sin(α − β) = cos²β − cos²α

Ans: Identities used: sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β and sin(α − β) = sin α cos β − cos α sin β.
L.H.S = sin(α + β) sin(α − β)
= (sin α cos β + cos α sin β)(sin α cos β − cos α sin β)
= sin²α cos²β − cos²α sin²β [difference of two squares]
= (1 − cos²α)cos²β − cos²α(1 − cos²β) [using sin²x = 1 − cos²x]
= cos²β − cos²α cos²β − cos²α + cos²α cos²β [expanding]
= cos²β − cos²α [the middle terms cancel]
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(i). Show that: cot(α + β) = (cot α cot β − 1)/(cot α + cot β)

Ans: Method: write cot(α + β) as (cos(α + β))/(sin(α + β)), expand, then divide numerator and denominator by sin α sin β.
L.H.S = cot(α + β) = (cos(α + β))/(sin(α + β))
= (cos α cos β − sin α sin β)/(sin α cos β + cos α sin β) [sum identities]
Divide every term of the numerator and the denominator by sin α sin β:
Numerator becomes: (cos α cos β)/(sin α sin β) − (sin α sin β)/(sin α sin β) = cot α cot β − 1
Denominator becomes: (sin α cos β)/(sin α sin β) + (cos α sin β)/(sin α sin β) = cot β + cot α
So L.H.S = (cot α cot β − 1)/(cot α + cot β)
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(ii). Show that: (sin(α + β))/(cos α cos β) = tan α + tan β

Ans: Identity used: sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β.
L.H.S = (sin(α + β))/(cos α cos β)
= (sin α cos β + cos α sin β)/(cos α cos β) [expanding sin(α + β)]
= (sin α cos β)/(cos α cos β) + (cos α sin β)/(cos α cos β) [splitting the fraction]
= (sin α)/(cos α) + (sin β)/(cos β) [cancelling cos β and cos α]
= tan α + tan β
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q8(i). Prove that: tan((π)/(4) + θ) = (cos θ + sin θ)/(cos θ − sin θ)

Ans: Identity used: tan(α + β) = (tan α + tan β)/(1 − tan α tan β), with tan((π)/(4)) = 1.
L.H.S = tan((π)/(4) + θ)
= (tan((π)/(4)) + tan θ)/(1 − tan((π)/(4)) tan θ)
= (1 + tan θ)/(1 − tan θ) [since tan((π)/(4)) = 1]
Now write tan θ = (sin θ)/(cos θ) and multiply numerator and denominator by cos θ:
= (cos θ + sin θ)/(cos θ − sin θ)
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q8(ii). Prove that: tan((π)/(4) − θ) = (1 − tan θ)/(1 + tan θ)

Ans: Identity used: tan(α − β) = (tan α − tan β)/(1 + tan α tan β), with tan((π)/(4)) = 1.
L.H.S = tan((π)/(4) − θ)
= (tan((π)/(4)) − tan θ)/(1 + tan((π)/(4)) tan θ)
= (1 − tan θ)/(1 + tan θ) [since tan((π)/(4)) = 1]
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q8(iii). Prove that: (tan(α + β))/(cot(α − β)) = (tan²α − tan²β)/(1 − tan²α tan²β)

Ans: Method: use (1)/(cot(α − β)) = tan(α − β), so the left side is a product of two tangents; then apply the tan sum and difference identities.
L.H.S = (tan(α + β))/(cot(α − β))
= tan(α + β) × tan(α − β) [since dividing by cot x is multiplying by tan x]
= ((tan α + tan β)/(1 − tan α tan β)) × ((tan α − tan β)/(1 + tan α tan β)) [tan sum and difference identities]
= ((tan α + tan β)(tan α − tan β))/((1 − tan α tan β)(1 + tan α tan β)) [combining the fractions]
= (tan²α − tan²β)/(1 − tan²α tan²β) [difference of two squares, top and bottom]
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q8(iv). Prove that: (1 − tan θ tan φ)/(1 + tan θ tan φ) = (cos(θ + φ))/(cos(θ − φ))

Ans: Method: work from the right hand side; expand cos(θ + φ) and cos(θ − φ), then divide numerator and denominator by cos θ cos φ.
R.H.S = (cos(θ + φ))/(cos(θ − φ))
= (cos θ cos φ − sin θ sin φ)/(cos θ cos φ + sin θ sin φ) [cos sum and difference identities]
Divide every term of the numerator and the denominator by cos θ cos φ:
Numerator becomes: 1 − (sin θ sin φ)/(cos θ cos φ) = 1 − tan θ tan φ
Denominator becomes: 1 + (sin θ sin φ)/(cos θ cos φ) = 1 + tan θ tan φ
So R.H.S = (1 − tan θ tan φ)/(1 + tan θ tan φ)
= L.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q9. Prove that: (sin θ)/(sec4θ) + (cos θ)/(cosec4θ) = sin5θ

Ans: Identities used: (1)/(sec x) = cos x and (1)/(cosec x) = sin x, then sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β.
L.H.S = (sin θ)/(sec4θ) + (cos θ)/(cosec4θ)
= sin θ cos4θ + cos θ sin4θ [using the reciprocal identities]
= sin(θ + 4θ) [by sin(α + β) with α = θ, β = 4θ, read backwards]
= sin5θ
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q10. Show that: (sin(180° − α) cos(270° − α))/(sin(180° + α) cos(270° + α)) = 1

Ans: Method: reduce each allied angle first, then simplify.
sin(180° − α) = sin α [sine is positive in Quadrant II]
cos(270° − α) = cos270° cos α + sin270° sin α = 0 − sin α = −sin α
sin(180° + α) = −sin α [sine is negative in Quadrant III]
cos(270° + α) = cos270° cos α − sin270° sin α = 0 + sin α = sin α
Substituting these values:
L.H.S = (sin α × (−sin α))/((−sin α) × (sin α))
= (−sin²α)/(−sin²α)
= 1
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q11. If α, β, γ are the angles of a ΔABC, show that: cot(α/2) + cot(β/2) + cot(γ/2) = cot(α/2) cot(β/2) cot(γ/2)

Ans: Since α, β, γ are the angles of a triangle, α + β + γ = 180°.
So (α)/(2) + (β)/(2) = 90° − (γ)/(2)
Taking tan of both sides: tan((α)/(2) + (β)/(2)) = tan(90° − (γ)/(2)) = cot((γ)/(2))
Using tan(x + y) = (tan x + tan y)/(1 − tan x tan y):
(tan(α/2) + tan(β/2))/(1 − tan(α/2) tan(β/2)) = (1)/(tan(γ/2)) [since cot x = (1)/(tan x)]
Cross-multiplying: tan((γ)/(2))(tan((α)/(2)) + tan((β)/(2))) = 1 − tan((α)/(2)) tan((β)/(2))
Expanding the left side: tan((α)/(2)) tan((γ)/(2)) + tan((β)/(2)) tan((γ)/(2)) = 1 − tan((α)/(2)) tan((β)/(2))
Bringing all products to the left: tan((α)/(2)) tan((β)/(2)) + tan((β)/(2)) tan((γ)/(2)) + tan((γ)/(2)) tan((α)/(2)) = 1 ... (1)
Divide both sides of (1) by tan((α)/(2)) tan((β)/(2)) tan((γ)/(2)):
Left side becomes: (1)/(tan(γ/2)) + (1)/(tan(α/2)) + (1)/(tan(β/2)) = cot((γ)/(2)) + cot((α)/(2)) + cot((β)/(2))
Right side becomes: (1)/(tan(α/2) tan(β/2) tan(γ/2)) = cot((α)/(2)) cot((β)/(2)) cot((γ)/(2))
Hence cot(α/2) + cot(β/2) + cot(γ/2) = cot(α/2) cot(β/2) cot(γ/2).
Hence proved.

Q: Q12. If α + β + γ = 180°, show that: cot α cot β + cot β cot γ + cot γ cot α = 1

Ans: From α + β + γ = 180°, we get α + β = 180° − γ.
Taking cot of both sides: cot(α + β) = cot(180° − γ) = −cot γ
Using cot(α + β) = (cot α cot β − 1)/(cot α + cot β):
(cot α cot β − 1)/(cot α + cot β) = −cot γ
Cross-multiplying: cot α cot β − 1 = −cot γ (cot α + cot β)
= −cot γ cot α − cot γ cot β [expanding]
Bringing the products to the left side: cot α cot β + cot β cot γ + cot γ cot α = 1
Hence proved.

Q: Q13(i). Express in the form r sin(θ + φ), where r > 0 and the terminal ray of φ is in the first quadrant: 4sinθ + 3cosθ

Ans: Method: write the expression as r sin(θ + φ) = r sin θ cos φ + r cos θ sin φ, so r cos φ = 4 and r sin φ = 3.
Squaring and adding: r²(cos²φ + sin²φ) = 4² + 3² = 25, so r² = 25 and r = 5
Then cos φ = (4)/(5) and sin φ = (3)/(5)
Both are positive, so φ is in the first quadrant, with φ ≈ 36.87°
Therefore 4sinθ + 3cosθ = 5 sin(θ + φ), where cos φ = (4)/(5), sin φ = (3)/(5)
Answer: 5 sin(θ + φ), where r = 5, cos φ = (4)/(5), sin φ = (3)/(5), φ ≈ 36.87°

Q: Q13(ii). Express in the form r sin(θ + φ), where r > 0 and the terminal ray of φ is in the first quadrant: 15sinθ + 8cosθ

Ans: Method: write the expression as r sin(θ + φ) = r sin θ cos φ + r cos θ sin φ, so r cos φ = 15 and r sin φ = 8.
Squaring and adding: r²(cos²φ + sin²φ) = 15² + 8² = 225 + 64 = 289, so r² = 289 and r = 17
Then cos φ = (15)/(17) and sin φ = (8)/(17)
Both are positive, so φ is in the first quadrant, with φ ≈ 28.07°
Therefore 15sinθ + 8cosθ = 17 sin(θ + φ), where cos φ = (15)/(17), sin φ = (8)/(17)
Answer: 17 sin(θ + φ), where r = 17, cos φ = (15)/(17), sin φ = (8)/(17), φ ≈ 28.07°

Q: Q13(iii). Express in the form r sin(θ + φ), where r > 0 and the terminal ray of φ is in the first quadrant: 2sinθ − 5cosθ

Ans: Method: write the expression as r sin(θ + φ) = r sin θ cos φ + r cos θ sin φ, so r cos φ = 2 and r sin φ = −5.
Squaring and adding: r²(cos²φ + sin²φ) = 2² + (−5)² = 4 + 25 = 29, so r² = 29 and r = √29
Then cos φ = (2)/(√29) and sin φ = −(5)/(√29)
Here sin φ is negative, so φ cannot lie in the first quadrant; φ ≈ −68.20°, i.e. φ is in the fourth quadrant, because the coefficient of cos θ is negative.
Therefore 2sinθ − 5cosθ = √29 sin(θ + φ), where cos φ = (2)/(√29), sin φ = −(5)/(√29)
Answer: √29 sin(θ + φ), where r = √29, cos φ = (2)/(√29), sin φ = −(5)/(√29), φ ≈ −68.20°

Q: Q13(iv). Express in the form r sin(θ + φ), where r > 0 and the terminal ray of φ is in the first quadrant: sinθ + cosθ

Ans: Method: write the expression as r sin(θ + φ) = r sin θ cos φ + r cos θ sin φ, so r cos φ = 1 and r sin φ = 1.
Squaring and adding: r²(cos²φ + sin²φ) = 1² + 1² = 2, so r² = 2 and r = √2
Then cos φ = (1)/(√2) and sin φ = (1)/(√2)
Both are positive, so φ is in the first quadrant, with φ = 45°
Therefore sinθ + cosθ = √2 sin(θ + φ), where cos φ = sin φ = (1)/(√2)
Answer: √2 sin(θ + 45°)

mcqs.why: tan α > 0 and α not in Quadrant I, so α is in Quadrant III: sin α = −(3)/(5), cos α = −(4)/(5). cos β = (5)/(13) > 0 and β not in Quadrant I, so β is in Quadrant IV: sin β = −(12)/(13). Then sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β = (−(3)/(5))((5)/(13)) + (−(4)/(5))(−(12)/(13)) = −(15)/(65) + (48)/(65) = (33)/(65).

mcqs.q: tan((π)/(4) + θ) is equal to:
options: (cos θ + sin θ)/(cos θ − sin θ)
(cos θ − sin θ)/(cos θ + sin θ)
mcqs.why: tan((π)/(4) + θ) = (tan((π)/(4)) + tan θ)/(1 − tan((π)/(4)) tan θ) = (1 + tan θ)/(1 − tan θ) since tan((π)/(4)) = 1. Writing tan θ = (sin θ)/(cos θ) and multiplying numerator and denominator by cos θ gives (cos θ + sin θ)/(cos θ − sin θ).

mcqs.q: In the form r sin(θ + φ), the expression 4sinθ + 3cosθ has r equal to:
mcqs.why: Compare r sin(θ + φ) = r sin θ cos φ + r cos θ sin φ, so r cos φ = 4 and r sin φ = 3. Squaring and adding: r²(cos²φ + sin²φ) = 4² + 3² = 25, so r² = 25 and r = 5 (r > 0).

lessons.title: Exercise 10.2
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • With tan θ = −(1)/(5): sin2θ = (2tan θ)/(1 + tan²θ) = −(5)/(13), cos2θ = (1 − tan²θ)/(1 + tan²θ) = (12)/(13), tan2θ = −(5)/(12).
  • With sin θ = (5)/(13) in Quadrant II, cos θ = −(12)/(13): sin2θ = −(120)/(169), cos2θ = (119)/(169), tan2θ = −(120)/(119).
  • With sin θ = (4)/(5) in Quadrant II, cos θ = −(3)/(5): sin2θ = −(24)/(25) and cos(θ/2) = (1)/(√5).
  • With cos θ = −(3)/(7) in Quadrant III: sin(θ/2) = √((5)/(7)) = (√5)/(√7).
  • sin(2π/3) = (√3)/(2) and cos(2π/3) = −(1)/(2) by the double-angle identities with x = (π)/(3).
  • Half-angle values: cos15° = (√(2 + √3))/(2) = (√6 + √2)/(4), tan67.5° = √2 + 1, sin112.5° = (√(2 + √2))/(2), cos(π/8) = (√(2 + √2))/(2).
  • cos⁴θ − sin⁴θ = cos2θ = (1)/(sec2θ), and (1 + cos2θ)/(1 − cos2θ) = cot²θ using 1 + cos2θ = 2cos²θ, 1 − cos2θ = 2sin²θ.
  • cos⁴θ = (3)/(8) + (1)/(2)cos2θ + (1)/(8)cos4θ by applying cos²θ = (1 + cos2θ)/(2) twice; sin4θ = 8sinθ cos³θ − 4sinθ cosθ.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. Find the values of sin2θ, cos2θ and tan2θ, given tan θ = −(1)/(5), θ in quadrant II.

Ans: Identities used (double-angle formulas in terms of tan θ): sin2θ = (2tan θ)/(1 + tan²θ), cos2θ = (1 − tan²θ)/(1 + tan²θ), tan2θ = (sin2θ)/(cos2θ).
First compute tan²θ = (−(1)/(5))² = (1)/(25)
sin2θ = (2tan θ)/(1 + tan²θ) = (2(−(1)/(5)))/(1 + (1)/(25))
= (−(2)/(5))/((26)/(25))
= −(2)/(5) × (25)/(26)
= −(10)/(26) = −(5)/(13)
cos2θ = (1 − tan²θ)/(1 + tan²θ) = (1 − (1)/(25))/(1 + (1)/(25))
= ((24)/(25))/((26)/(25))
= (24)/(26) = (12)/(13)
tan2θ = (sin2θ)/(cos2θ) = (−(5)/(13))/((12)/(13)) = −(5)/(12)
Answer: sin2θ = −(5)/(13), cos2θ = (12)/(13), tan2θ = −(5)/(12)

Q: Q2(i). If sin θ = (5)/(13) and the terminal ray of θ is in the second quadrant, find: sin2θ

Ans: First find cos θ using sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ = 1 − (25)/(169) = (144)/(169)
θ is in the second quadrant, where cosine is negative, so cos θ = −(12)/(13)
Identity used: sin2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ
sin2θ = 2 × (5)/(13) × (−(12)/(13))
= −(120)/(169)
Answer: sin2θ = −(120)/(169)

Q: Q2(ii). If sin θ = (5)/(13) and the terminal ray of θ is in the second quadrant, find: cos2θ

Ans: First find cos θ using sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
cos²θ = 1 − (25)/(169) = (144)/(169); θ is in the second quadrant, so cos θ = −(12)/(13)
Identity used: cos2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ
cos2θ = (144)/(169) − (25)/(169)
= (119)/(169)
Answer: cos2θ = (119)/(169)

Q: Q2(iii). If sin θ = (5)/(13) and the terminal ray of θ is in the second quadrant, find: tan2θ

Ans: From the companion parts, sin2θ = −(120)/(169) and cos2θ = (119)/(169) (using cos θ = −(12)/(13), since θ is in the second quadrant).
Identity used: tan2θ = (sin2θ)/(cos2θ)
tan2θ = (−(120)/(169))/((119)/(169))
= −(120)/(119)
Answer: tan2θ = −(120)/(119)

Q: Q3(i). If sin θ = (4)/(5) and the terminal ray of θ is in the second quadrant, find: sin2θ

Ans: First find cos θ using sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ = 1 − (16)/(25) = (9)/(25)
θ is in the second quadrant, where cosine is negative, so cos θ = −(3)/(5)
Identity used: sin2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ
sin2θ = 2 × (4)/(5) × (−(3)/(5))
= −(24)/(25)
Answer: sin2θ = −(24)/(25)

Q: Q3(ii). If sin θ = (4)/(5) and the terminal ray of θ is in the second quadrant, find: cos(θ/2)

Ans: First find cos θ using sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
cos²θ = 1 − (16)/(25) = (9)/(25); θ is in the second quadrant, so cos θ = −(3)/(5)
Since θ is in the second quadrant, (θ)/(2) is in the first quadrant, where cosine is positive.
Identity used (half-angle): cos(θ/2) = √((1 + cos θ)/(2)), taking the positive root
cos(θ/2) = √((1 + (−(3)/(5)))/(2))
= √(((2)/(5))/(2))
= √((1)/(5))
= (1)/(√5)
Answer: cos(θ/2) = (1)/(√5)

Q: Q4. If cos θ = −(3)/(7) and the terminal ray of θ is in the 3rd quadrant, find sin(θ/2).

Ans: Since θ is in the third quadrant, (θ)/(2) is in the second quadrant, where sine is positive.
Identity used (half-angle): sin(θ/2) = √((1 − cos θ)/(2)), taking the positive root
sin(θ/2) = √((1 − (−(3)/(7)))/(2))
= √(((10)/(7))/(2))
= √((5)/(7))
= (√5)/(√7)
Answer: sin(θ/2) = (√5)/(√7) ≈ 0.845

Q: Q5(i). Use double angle identities to evaluate exactly: sin(2π/3)

Ans: Method: write (2π)/(3) = 2 × (π)/(3) and use sin2x = 2 sin x cos x with x = (π)/(3).
sin(2π/3) = sin(2 × (π)/(3))
= 2 sin((π)/(3)) cos((π)/(3)) [by sin2x identity]
= 2 × ((√3)/(2)) × ((1)/(2))
= (√3)/(2)
Answer: (√3)/(2)

Q: Q5(ii). Use double angle identities to evaluate exactly: cos(2π/3)

Ans: Method: write (2π)/(3) = 2 × (π)/(3) and use cos2x = cos²x − sin²x with x = (π)/(3).
cos(2π/3) = cos(2 × (π)/(3))
= cos²((π)/(3)) − sin²((π)/(3)) [by cos2x identity]
= ((1)/(2))² − ((√3)/(2))²
= (1)/(4) − (3)/(4)
= −(1)/(2)
Answer: −(1)/(2)

Q: Q6(i). Use the half-angle identities to evaluate exactly: cos15°

Ans: Method: 15° is half of 30°, so use cos(θ/2) = √((1 + cos θ)/(2)) with θ = 30°; 15° is in the first quadrant, so take the positive root.
cos15° = √((1 + cos30°)/(2))
= √((1 + (√3)/(2))/(2))
= √((2 + √3)/(4))
= (√(2 + √3))/(2)
This can also be written in the form (√6 + √2)/(4), since ((√6 + √2)/(4))² = (2 + √3)/(4).
Answer: (√(2 + √3))/(2) = (√6 + √2)/(4)

Q: Q6(ii). Use the half-angle identities to evaluate exactly: tan67.5°

Ans: Method: 67.5° is half of 135°, so use tan(θ/2) = (1 − cos θ)/(sin θ) with θ = 135°, where cos135° = −(√2)/(2) and sin135° = (√2)/(2).
tan67.5° = (1 − cos135°)/(sin135°)
= (1 − (−(√2)/(2)))/((√2)/(2))
= (1 + (√2)/(2))/((√2)/(2))
= ((2 + √2)/(2))/((√2)/(2))
= (2 + √2)/(√2)
= √2 + 1 [dividing term by term: (2)/(√2) = √2 and (√2)/(√2) = 1]
Answer: √2 + 1 (the book's key writes this as √(3 + 2√2), which is equal to √2 + 1)

Q: Q6(iii). Use the half-angle identities to evaluate exactly: sin112.5°

Ans: Method: 112.5° is half of 225°, so use sin(θ/2) = √((1 − cos θ)/(2)) with θ = 225°, where cos225° = −(√2)/(2); 112.5° is in the second quadrant, where sine is positive.
sin112.5° = √((1 − cos225°)/(2))
= √((1 − (−(√2)/(2)))/(2))
= √((1 + (√2)/(2))/(2))
= √((2 + √2)/(4))
= (√(2 + √2))/(2)
Answer: (√(2 + √2))/(2)

Q: Q6(iv). Use the half-angle identities to evaluate exactly: cos(π/8)

Ans: Method: (π)/(8) is half of (π)/(4), so use cos(θ/2) = √((1 + cos θ)/(2)) with θ = (π)/(4), where cos((π)/(4)) = (√2)/(2); (π)/(8) is in the first quadrant, so take the positive root.
cos(π/8) = √((1 + cos(π/4))/(2))
= √((1 + (√2)/(2))/(2))
= √((2 + √2)/(4))
= (√(2 + √2))/(2)
Answer: (√(2 + √2))/(2)

Q: Q6(v). Use the half-angle identities to evaluate exactly: tan75°

Ans: Method: 75° is half of 150°, so use tan(θ/2) = (1 − cos θ)/(sin θ) with θ = 150°, where cos150° = −(√3)/(2) and sin150° = (1)/(2).
tan75° = (1 − cos150°)/(sin150°)
= (1 − (−(√3)/(2)))/((1)/(2))
= (1 + (√3)/(2))/((1)/(2))
= 2 + √3 [multiplying numerator and denominator by 2]
Answer: 2 + √3 (the book's key writes this as √(7 + 4√3), which is equal to 2 + √3)

Q: Q6(vi). Use the half-angle identities to evaluate exactly: sin(5π/12)

Ans: Method: (5π)/(12) = 75°, which is half of 150°, so use sin(θ/2) = √((1 − cos θ)/(2)) with θ = 150°, where cos150° = −(√3)/(2); 75° is in the first quadrant, so take the positive root.
sin(5π/12) = sin75°
= √((1 − cos150°)/(2))
= √((1 − (−(√3)/(2)))/(2))
= √((1 + (√3)/(2))/(2))
= √((2 + √3)/(4))
= (√(2 + √3))/(2)
This can also be written as (√6 + √2)/(4).
Answer: (√(2 + √3))/(2) = (√6 + √2)/(4)

Q: Q7(i). Prove the identity: cos⁴θ − sin⁴θ = (1)/(sec2θ)

Ans: Method: factorise the left side as a difference of two squares and use cos2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ and (1)/(sec x) = cos x.
L.H.S = cos⁴θ − sin⁴θ
= (cos²θ − sin²θ)(cos²θ + sin²θ) [difference of two squares]
= (cos²θ − sin²θ)(1) [since cos²θ + sin²θ = 1]
= cos2θ [by the double-angle identity]
= (1)/(sec2θ) [reciprocal identity]
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(ii). Prove the identity: tan(θ/2) + cot(θ/2) = (2)/(sin θ)

Ans: Method: write tan and cot in terms of sine and cosine of (θ)/(2), combine, and use sin θ = 2 sin(θ/2) cos(θ/2).
L.H.S = tan(θ/2) + cot(θ/2)
= (sin(θ/2))/(cos(θ/2)) + (cos(θ/2))/(sin(θ/2))
= (sin²(θ/2) + cos²(θ/2))/(sin(θ/2) cos(θ/2)) [taking the common denominator]
= (1)/(sin(θ/2) cos(θ/2)) [since sin²x + cos²x = 1]
Now sin(θ/2) cos(θ/2) = (1)/(2) sin θ [from sin θ = 2 sin(θ/2) cos(θ/2)]
So L.H.S = (1)/((1)/(2) sin θ)
= (2)/(sin θ)
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(iii). Prove the identity: (1 + cos2θ)/(1 − cos2θ) = cot²θ

Ans: Identities used: 1 + cos2θ = 2cos²θ and 1 − cos2θ = 2sin²θ.
L.H.S = (1 + cos2θ)/(1 − cos2θ)
= (2cos²θ)/(2sin²θ) [by the two identities above]
= (cos²θ)/(sin²θ) [cancelling 2]
= cot²θ [since cot θ = (cos θ)/(sin θ)]
= R.H.S
Hence proved.
Note: In the book the denominator of this question is misprinted as 1 + cos2θ (the same as the numerator), which would make the left side equal to 1; the intended denominator is 1 − cos2θ, as proved above.

Q: Q7(iv). Prove the identity: cosec2θ − cot2θ = tan θ

Ans: Method: write cosec2θ = (1)/(sin2θ) and cot2θ = (cos2θ)/(sin2θ), then use 1 − cos2θ = 2sin²θ and sin2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ.
L.H.S = cosec2θ − cot2θ
= (1)/(sin2θ) − (cos2θ)/(sin2θ)
= (1 − cos2θ)/(sin2θ) [common denominator]
= (2sin²θ)/(2 sin θ cos θ) [by the identities above]
= (sin θ)/(cos θ) [cancelling 2 sin θ]
= tan θ
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(v). Prove the identity: (sin3β)/(sin β) − (cos3β)/(cos β) = 2

Ans: Identities used: sin3β = 3 sin β − 4sin³β and cos3β = 4cos³β − 3 cos β.
L.H.S = (sin3β)/(sin β) − (cos3β)/(cos β)
= (3 sin β − 4sin³β)/(sin β) − (4cos³β − 3 cos β)/(cos β) [substituting the triple-angle formulas]
= (3 − 4sin²β) − (4cos²β − 3) [dividing each term]
= 3 − 4sin²β − 4cos²β + 3 [expanding]
= 6 − 4(sin²β + cos²β) [grouping]
= 6 − 4(1) [since sin²β + cos²β = 1]
= 2
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(vi). Prove the identity: (sin3θ)/(cos θ) + (cos3θ)/(sin θ) = 2cot2θ

Ans: Method: take the common denominator sin θ cos θ and use cos(A − B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B in the numerator.
L.H.S = (sin3θ)/(cos θ) + (cos3θ)/(sin θ)
= (sin3θ sin θ + cos3θ cos θ)/(sin θ cos θ) [common denominator]
= (cos(3θ − θ))/(sin θ cos θ) [numerator is cos(A − B) with A = 3θ, B = θ]
= (cos2θ)/(sin θ cos θ)
Now sin θ cos θ = (1)/(2) sin2θ [from sin2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ]
So L.H.S = (cos2θ)/((1)/(2) sin2θ)
= 2 (cos2θ)/(sin2θ)
= 2cot2θ
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(vii). Prove the identity: (cos³θ − sin³θ)/(cos θ − sin θ) = (2 + sin2θ)/(2)

Ans: Method: factorise the numerator using a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²), then use sin2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ.
L.H.S = (cos³θ − sin³θ)/(cos θ − sin θ)
= ((cos θ − sin θ)(cos²θ + cos θ sin θ + sin²θ))/(cos θ − sin θ) [factorising]
= cos²θ + sin²θ + sin θ cos θ [cancelling (cos θ − sin θ)]
= 1 + sin θ cos θ [since cos²θ + sin²θ = 1]
= 1 + (1)/(2) sin2θ [since sin θ cos θ = (1)/(2) sin2θ]
= (2 + sin2θ)/(2) [writing over the common denominator 2]
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(viii). Prove the identity: (2cos³θ)/(1 − sin θ) = 2cos θ + sin2θ

Ans: Method: work from the left side; write cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ and factorise, then use sin2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ.
L.H.S = (2cos³θ)/(1 − sin θ)
= (2 cos θ × cos²θ)/(1 − sin θ)
= (2 cos θ (1 − sin²θ))/(1 − sin θ) [using cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ]
= (2 cos θ (1 − sin θ)(1 + sin θ))/(1 − sin θ) [difference of two squares]
= 2 cos θ (1 + sin θ) [cancelling (1 − sin θ)]
= 2 cos θ + 2 sin θ cos θ [expanding]
= 2 cos θ + sin2θ [since 2 sin θ cos θ = sin2θ]
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(ix). Prove the identity: cot2θ = (1)/(2)(cot θ − (1)/(cot θ))

Ans: Method: work from the right side; use (1)/(cot θ) = tan θ, write in sines and cosines, and use the double-angle identities.
R.H.S = (1)/(2)(cot θ − (1)/(cot θ))
= (1)/(2)(cot θ − tan θ) [since (1)/(cot θ) = tan θ]
= (1)/(2)((cos θ)/(sin θ) − (sin θ)/(cos θ))
= (1)/(2) × (cos²θ − sin²θ)/(sin θ cos θ) [common denominator]
= (1)/(2) × (cos2θ)/((1)/(2) sin2θ) [using cos²θ − sin²θ = cos2θ and sin θ cos θ = (1)/(2) sin2θ]
= (cos2θ)/(sin2θ)
= cot2θ
= L.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(x). Prove the identity: (sin α + cos α)/(cos α − sin α) + (sin α − cos α)/(cos α + sin α) = 2tan2α

Ans: Method: take the common denominator (cos α − sin α)(cos α + sin α) = cos²α − sin²α = cos2α and simplify the numerator.
L.H.S = (sin α + cos α)/(cos α − sin α) + (sin α − cos α)/(cos α + sin α)
= ((sin α + cos α)² + (sin α − cos α)(cos α − sin α))/((cos α − sin α)(cos α + sin α)) [common denominator]
Numerator: (sin α + cos α)² = 1 + 2 sin α cos α = 1 + sin2α
Numerator: (sin α − cos α)(cos α − sin α) = −(sin α − cos α)² = −(1 − 2 sin α cos α) = sin2α − 1
So the whole numerator = (1 + sin2α) + (sin2α − 1) = 2 sin2α
Denominator = cos²α − sin²α = cos2α
So L.H.S = (2 sin2α)/(cos2α)
= 2tan2α
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(xi). Prove the identity: tan(α/2) = (sin α)/(1 + cos α)

Ans: Method: work from the right side using sin α = 2 sin(α/2) cos(α/2) and 1 + cos α = 2cos²(α/2).
R.H.S = (sin α)/(1 + cos α)
= (2 sin(α/2) cos(α/2))/(2cos²(α/2)) [by the two identities above]
= (sin(α/2))/(cos(α/2)) [cancelling 2 cos(α/2)]
= tan(α/2)
= L.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(xii). Prove the identity: (cosec θ − cot θ)/(1 + cos θ) = cosec θ tan²(θ/2)

Ans: Method: work from the right side using tan²(θ/2) = (1 − cos θ)/(1 + cos θ).
R.H.S = cosec θ tan²(θ/2)
= cosec θ × (1 − cos θ)/(1 + cos θ) [half-angle identity for tan²(θ/2)]
= ((1)/(sin θ)) × (1 − cos θ)/(1 + cos θ)
= (1 − cos θ)/(sin θ (1 + cos θ))
Now divide the numerator and denominator of the left side form: (cosec θ − cot θ) = (1)/(sin θ) − (cos θ)/(sin θ) = (1 − cos θ)/(sin θ)
So (cosec θ − cot θ)/(1 + cos θ) = ((1 − cos θ)/(sin θ))/(1 + cos θ) = (1 − cos θ)/(sin θ (1 + cos θ)), which is the same as above.
Hence R.H.S = L.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(xiii). Prove the identity: cos²(θ/2) = (1 − cos²θ)/(2 − 2cos θ)

Ans: Method: work from the right side; write 1 − cos²θ = sin²θ = (1 − cos θ)(1 + cos θ) and use cos²(θ/2) = (1 + cos θ)/(2).
R.H.S = (1 − cos²θ)/(2 − 2cos θ)
= ((1 − cos θ)(1 + cos θ))/(2(1 − cos θ)) [factorising numerator and denominator]
= (1 + cos θ)/(2) [cancelling (1 − cos θ)]
= cos²(θ/2) [half-angle identity]
= L.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(xiv). Prove the identity: (1 − tan²(α/2))/(1 + tan²(α/2)) = cos α

Ans: Method: multiply numerator and denominator by cos²(α/2) and use cos²x − sin²x = cos2x.
L.H.S = (1 − tan²(α/2))/(1 + tan²(α/2))
Multiply numerator and denominator by cos²(α/2):
Numerator becomes: cos²(α/2) − sin²(α/2) [since tan²(α/2) cos²(α/2) = sin²(α/2)]
Denominator becomes: cos²(α/2) + sin²(α/2) = 1
So L.H.S = (cos²(α/2) − sin²(α/2))/(1)
= cos α [by cos2x = cos²x − sin²x with x = (α)/(2)]
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q7(xv). Prove the identity: sin2θ − 4sin³θ cos θ = sin2θ cos2θ

Ans: Method: factor out sin2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ from the left side and use cos2θ = 1 − 2sin²θ.
L.H.S = sin2θ − 4sin³θ cos θ
= 2 sin θ cos θ − 4sin³θ cos θ [using sin2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ]
= 2 sin θ cos θ (1 − 2sin²θ) [taking out the common factor 2 sin θ cos θ]
= sin2θ × cos2θ [since 2 sin θ cos θ = sin2θ and 1 − 2sin²θ = cos2θ]
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q8. Write cos⁴θ in terms of the first power of one or more cosine functions.

Ans: Method: use cos²θ = (1 + cos2θ)/(2) twice (power-reduction).
cos⁴θ = (cos²θ)²
= ((1 + cos2θ)/(2))² [first use of the identity]
= (1)/(4)(1 + 2cos2θ + cos²2θ) [squaring]
Now use the identity again on cos²2θ, with 2θ in place of θ: cos²2θ = (1 + cos4θ)/(2)
cos⁴θ = (1)/(4)(1 + 2cos2θ + (1 + cos4θ)/(2))
= (1)/(4)((3)/(2) + 2cos2θ + (1)/(2) cos4θ) [combining the constant terms: 1 + (1)/(2) = (3)/(2)]
= (3)/(8) + (1)/(2) cos2θ + (1)/(8) cos4θ
Answer: cos⁴θ = (3)/(8) + (1)/(2)cos2θ + (1)/(8)cos4θ

Q: Q9(i). Prove the identity: sin4θ = 8sinθ cos³θ − 4sinθ cosθ

Ans: Method: write 4θ = 2(2θ) and apply the double-angle identities step by step.
L.H.S = sin4θ = sin(2(2θ))
= 2 sin2θ cos2θ [by sin2x = 2 sin x cos x with x = 2θ]
= 2(2 sin θ cos θ)(2cos²θ − 1) [using sin2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ and cos2θ = 2cos²θ − 1]
= 4 sin θ cos θ (2cos²θ − 1) [simplifying]
= 8sinθ cos³θ − 4sinθ cosθ [expanding]
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q9(ii). Prove the identity: cot4θ = (1 − tan²2θ)/(2tan2θ)

Ans: Method: use cot4θ = (1)/(tan4θ) and the double-angle formula tan2x = (2tan x)/(1 − tan²x) with x = 2θ.
R.H.S = (1 − tan²2θ)/(2tan2θ)
= 1 ÷ ((2tan2θ)/(1 − tan²2θ))
But (2tan2θ)/(1 − tan²2θ) = tan(2 × 2θ) = tan4θ [by the tan double-angle formula]
So R.H.S = (1)/(tan4θ)
= cot4θ
= L.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q9(iii). Prove the identity: cot3θ = (cot³θ − 3cot θ)/(3cot²θ − 1)

Ans: Method: start from the triple-angle formula tan3θ = (3tan θ − tan³θ)/(1 − 3tan²θ), take the reciprocal, and divide numerator and denominator by tan³θ.
cot3θ = (1)/(tan3θ)
= (1 − 3tan²θ)/(3tan θ − tan³θ) [taking the reciprocal of tan3θ]
Divide every term of the numerator and the denominator by tan³θ:
Numerator becomes: (1)/(tan³θ) − (3)/(tan θ) = cot³θ − 3cot θ
Denominator becomes: (3)/(tan²θ) − 1 = 3cot²θ − 1
So cot3θ = (cot³θ − 3cot θ)/(3cot²θ − 1)
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.3
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • 2sin6x sinx = cos5x − cos7x by 2 sin α sin β = cos(α − β) − cos(α + β).
  • sin55° cos123° = (1)/(2)[sin178° − sin68°] by sin α cos β = (1)/(2)[sin(α + β) + sin(α − β)].
  • sin37° + sin43° = 2 sin40° cos3° and cos36° − cos82° = 2 sin59° sin23° by the sum-to-product identities.
  • (cos75° + cos15°)/(sin75° − sin15°) = cot30° = √3.
  • (sin α + sin9α)/(cos α + cos9α) = tan5α, since numerator = 2 sin5α cos4α and denominator = 2 cos5α cos4α.
  • (sin135° − cos120°)/(sin135° + cos120°) = (√2 + 1)/(√2 − 1) = 3 + 2√2.
  • cos20° cos40° cos60° cos80° = (1)/(16) and sin10° sin30° sin50° sin70° = (1)/(16).
  • sin(π/9) sin(2π/9) sin(π/3) sin(4π/9) = sin20° sin40° sin60° sin80° = (3)/(16).

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Express the product as a sum or difference: 2sin6x sinx

Ans: Identity used: 2 sin α sin β = cos(α − β) − cos(α + β)
Here α = 6x and β = x.
2sin6x sinx = cos(6x − x) − cos(6x + x)
= cos5x − cos7x
Answer: cos5x − cos7x

Q: Q1(ii). Express the product as a sum or difference: sin55° cos123°

Ans: Identity used: sin α cos β = (1)/(2)[sin(α + β) + sin(α − β)]
Here α = 55° and β = 123°.
sin55° cos123° = (1)/(2)[sin(55° + 123°) + sin(55° − 123°)]
= (1)/(2)[sin178° + sin(−68°)]
= (1)/(2)[sin178° − sin68°] [since sin(−x) = −sin x]
Answer: (1)/(2)[sin178° − sin68°]
Note: The book's printed answer ((1)/(2)[sin178° − sin66°]) is incorrect; the correct answer is (1)/(2)[sin178° − sin68°].

Q: Q1(iii). Express the product as a sum or difference: sin((A + B)/2) cos((A − B)/2)

Ans: Identity used: sin α cos β = (1)/(2)[sin(α + β) + sin(α − β)]
Here α = ((A + B))/(2) and β = ((A − B))/(2).
α + β = ((A + B) + (A − B))/(2) = (2A)/(2) = A
α − β = ((A + B) − (A − B))/(2) = (2B)/(2) = B
So sin((A + B)/2) cos((A − B)/2) = (1)/(2)[sin A + sin B]
Answer: (1)/(2)(sin A + sin B)

Q: Q1(iv). Express the product as a sum or difference: cos((P + Q)/2) cos((P − Q)/2)

Ans: Identity used: cos α cos β = (1)/(2)[cos(α + β) + cos(α − β)]
Here α = ((P + Q))/(2) and β = ((P − Q))/(2).
α + β = ((P + Q) + (P − Q))/(2) = (2P)/(2) = P
α − β = ((P + Q) − (P − Q))/(2) = (2Q)/(2) = Q
So cos((P + Q)/2) cos((P − Q)/2) = (1)/(2)[cos P + cos Q]
Answer: (1)/(2)(cos P + cos Q)

Q: Q2(i). Express the sum or difference as a product: sin37° + sin43°

Ans: Identity used: sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C + D)/(2)) cos((C − D)/(2))
Here C = 37° and D = 43°.
(C + D)/(2) = (37° + 43°)/(2) = 40°
(C − D)/(2) = (37° − 43°)/(2) = −3°, and cos(−3°) = cos3°
sin37° + sin43° = 2 sin40° cos3°
Answer: 2 sin40° cos3°

Q: Q2(ii). Express the sum or difference as a product: cos36° − cos82°

Ans: Identity used: cos C − cos D = −2 sin((C + D)/(2)) sin((C − D)/(2))
Here C = 36° and D = 82°.
(C + D)/(2) = (36° + 82°)/(2) = 59°
(C − D)/(2) = (36° − 82°)/(2) = −23°
cos36° − cos82° = −2 sin59° sin(−23°)
= 2 sin59° sin23° [since sin(−x) = −sin x]
Answer: 2 sin59° sin23°
Note: The book's printed answer (−2 sin59° sin23°) is incorrect; the correct answer is 2 sin59° sin23°.

Q: Q2(iii). Express the sum or difference as a product: sin((P + Q)/2) − sin((P − Q)/2)

Ans: Identity used: sin C − sin D = 2 cos((C + D)/(2)) sin((C − D)/(2))
Here C = ((P + Q))/(2) and D = ((P − Q))/(2).
(C + D)/(2) = (((P + Q) + (P − Q))/(2))/(2) = (2P)/(4) = (P)/(2)
(C − D)/(2) = (((P + Q) − (P − Q))/(2))/(2) = (2Q)/(4) = (Q)/(2)
So sin((P + Q)/2) − sin((P − Q)/2) = 2 cos((P)/(2)) sin((Q)/(2))
Answer: 2 cos(P/2) sin(Q/2)

Q: Q2(iv). Express the sum or difference as a product: cos((A + B)/2) + cos((A − B)/2)

Ans: Identity used: cos C + cos D = 2 cos((C + D)/(2)) cos((C − D)/(2))
Here C = ((A + B))/(2) and D = ((A − B))/(2).
(C + D)/(2) = (((A + B) + (A − B))/(2))/(2) = (2A)/(4) = (A)/(2)
(C − D)/(2) = (((A + B) − (A − B))/(2))/(2) = (2B)/(4) = (B)/(2)
So cos((A + B)/2) + cos((A − B)/2) = 2 cos((A)/(2)) cos((B)/(2))
Answer: 2 cos(A/2) cos(B/2)

Q: Q3(i). Prove that: (cos75° + cos15°)/(sin75° − sin15°) = √3

Ans: Identities used: cos C + cos D = 2 cos((C + D)/(2)) cos((C − D)/(2)) and sin C − sin D = 2 cos((C + D)/(2)) sin((C − D)/(2)).
Numerator: cos75° + cos15° = 2 cos((75° + 15°)/(2)) cos((75° − 15°)/(2)) = 2 cos45° cos30°
Denominator: sin75° − sin15° = 2 cos((75° + 15°)/(2)) sin((75° − 15°)/(2)) = 2 cos45° sin30°
L.H.S = (2 cos45° cos30°)/(2 cos45° sin30°)
= (cos30°)/(sin30°) [cancelling 2 cos45°]
= cot30°
= √3
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q3(ii). Prove that: (sin135° − cos120°)/(sin135° + cos120°) = 3 + 2√2

Ans: Method: substitute the exact values sin135° = (√2)/(2) and cos120° = −(1)/(2), then rationalise.
L.H.S = (sin135° − cos120°)/(sin135° + cos120°)
= ((√2)/(2) − (−(1)/(2)))/((√2)/(2) + (−(1)/(2))) [substituting the values]
= ((√2)/(2) + (1)/(2))/((√2)/(2) − (1)/(2))
= (√2 + 1)/(√2 − 1) [multiplying numerator and denominator by 2]
Rationalise by multiplying numerator and denominator by (√2 + 1):
= ((√2 + 1)²)/((√2)² − 1²)
= (2 + 2√2 + 1)/(2 − 1)
= (3 + 2√2)/(1)
= 3 + 2√2
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(i). Prove that: (sin α + sin9α)/(cos α + cos9α) = tan5α

Ans: Identities used: sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C + D)/(2)) cos((C − D)/(2)) and cos C + cos D = 2 cos((C + D)/(2)) cos((C − D)/(2)).
Numerator: sin α + sin9α = 2 sin((α + 9α)/(2)) cos((9α − α)/(2)) = 2 sin5α cos4α
Denominator: cos α + cos9α = 2 cos((α + 9α)/(2)) cos((9α − α)/(2)) = 2 cos5α cos4α
L.H.S = (2 sin5α cos4α)/(2 cos5α cos4α)
= (sin5α)/(cos5α) [cancelling 2 cos4α]
= tan5α
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(ii). Prove that: (cos β + cos3β + cos5β)/(sin β + sin3β + sin5β) = cot3β

Ans: Method: group the first and last terms in the numerator and denominator and use the sum-to-product identities.
Numerator: cos β + cos5β = 2 cos((β + 5β)/(2)) cos((5β − β)/(2)) = 2 cos3β cos2β [by cos C + cos D identity]
So numerator = 2 cos3β cos2β + cos3β = cos3β (2cos2β + 1) [taking out cos3β]
Denominator: sin β + sin5β = 2 sin((β + 5β)/(2)) cos((5β − β)/(2)) = 2 sin3β cos2β [by sin C + sin D identity]
So denominator = 2 sin3β cos2β + sin3β = sin3β (2cos2β + 1) [taking out sin3β]
L.H.S = (cos3β (2cos2β + 1))/(sin3β (2cos2β + 1))
= (cos3β)/(sin3β) [cancelling (2cos2β + 1)]
= cot3β
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(iii). Prove that: sin2θ + sin4θ + sin6θ = 4cosθ cos2θ sin3θ

Ans: Method: group sin2θ + sin4θ using sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C + D)/(2)) cos((C − D)/(2)), then factor.
L.H.S = sin2θ + sin4θ + sin6θ
= 2 sin((2θ + 4θ)/(2)) cos((4θ − 2θ)/(2)) + sin6θ [grouping the first two terms]
= 2 sin3θ cos θ + sin6θ
Now sin6θ = 2 sin3θ cos3θ [by sin2x = 2 sin x cos x with x = 3θ]
So L.H.S = 2 sin3θ cos θ + 2 sin3θ cos3θ
= 2 sin3θ (cos θ + cos3θ) [taking out 2 sin3θ]
= 2 sin3θ × 2 cos((θ + 3θ)/(2)) cos((3θ − θ)/(2)) [by cos C + cos D identity]
= 2 sin3θ × 2 cos2θ cos θ
= 4 cos θ cos2θ sin3θ
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(iv). Prove that: sin5θ + sinθ + 2sin3θ = 4sin3θ cos²θ

Ans: Method: group sin5θ + sin θ using sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C + D)/(2)) cos((C − D)/(2)), then use 1 + cos2θ = 2cos²θ.
L.H.S = sin5θ + sinθ + 2sin3θ
= 2 sin((5θ + θ)/(2)) cos((5θ − θ)/(2)) + 2sin3θ [grouping the first two terms]
= 2 sin3θ cos2θ + 2 sin3θ
= 2 sin3θ (cos2θ + 1) [taking out 2 sin3θ]
= 2 sin3θ × 2cos²θ [using 1 + cos2θ = 2cos²θ]
= 4 sin3θ cos²θ
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(v). Prove that: sin3θ + sin5θ + sin7θ + sin9θ = 4cosθ sin6θ cos2θ

Ans: Method: group (sin3θ + sin9θ) and (sin5θ + sin7θ) using sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C + D)/(2)) cos((C − D)/(2)).
sin3θ + sin9θ = 2 sin((3θ + 9θ)/(2)) cos((9θ − 3θ)/(2)) = 2 sin6θ cos3θ
sin5θ + sin7θ = 2 sin((5θ + 7θ)/(2)) cos((7θ − 5θ)/(2)) = 2 sin6θ cos θ
L.H.S = 2 sin6θ cos3θ + 2 sin6θ cos θ
= 2 sin6θ (cos3θ + cos θ) [taking out 2 sin6θ]
= 2 sin6θ × 2 cos((3θ + θ)/(2)) cos((3θ − θ)/(2)) [by cos C + cos D identity]
= 2 sin6θ × 2 cos2θ cos θ
= 4 cos θ sin6θ cos2θ
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(vi). Prove that: cos β + cos2β + cos5β = cos2β (1 + 2cos3β)

Ans: Method: work from the right side and use 2 cos A cos B = cos(A + B) + cos(A − B).
R.H.S = cos2β (1 + 2cos3β)
= cos2β + 2cos2β cos3β [expanding]
Now 2cos2β cos3β = cos(3β + 2β) + cos(3β − 2β) = cos5β + cos β [product-to-sum identity]
So R.H.S = cos2β + cos5β + cos β
= cos β + cos2β + cos5β [rearranging]
= L.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q5(i). Prove that: cos20° cos40° cos60° cos80° = (1)/(16)

Ans: Method: use cos60° = (1)/(2), then multiply the remaining product by (sin20°)/(sin20°) and use sin2x = 2 sin x cos x repeatedly.
L.H.S = cos20° cos40° cos60° cos80°
= (1)/(2) × cos20° cos40° cos80° [since cos60° = (1)/(2)]
Let P = cos20° cos40° cos80°. Multiply P by 8sin20°:
8sin20° × P = (2sin20° cos20°) × (2cos40°) × (2cos80°)
2sin20° cos20° = sin40°, so this becomes (2sin40° cos40°) × (2cos80°)
2sin40° cos40° = sin80°, so this becomes 2sin80° cos80°
2sin80° cos80° = sin160° = sin(180° − 20°) = sin20°
So 8sin20° × P = sin20°, giving P = (1)/(8)
Therefore L.H.S = (1)/(2) × (1)/(8) = (1)/(16)
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q5(ii). Prove that: sin(π/9) sin(2π/9) sin(π/3) sin(4π/9) = (3)/(16)

Ans: Method: convert to degrees: (π)/(9) = 20°, (2π)/(9) = 40°, (π)/(3) = 60°, (4π)/(9) = 80°; then use product-to-sum identities.
L.H.S = sin20° sin40° sin60° sin80°
sin60° = (√3)/(2)
First find sin40° sin80° = (1)/(2)[cos(40° − 80°) − cos(40° + 80°)] [by sin α sin β identity]
= (1)/(2)[cos40° − cos120°] [since cos(−40°) = cos40°]
= (1)/(2)[cos40° + (1)/(2)] [since cos120° = −(1)/(2)]
Multiply by sin20°: sin20° sin40° sin80° = (1)/(2) sin20° cos40° + (1)/(4) sin20°
Now 2 sin20° cos40° = sin(20° + 40°) + sin(20° − 40°) = sin60° − sin20° [by 2 sin α cos β identity]
So sin20° sin40° sin80° = (1)/(4)(sin60° − sin20°) + (1)/(4) sin20° = (1)/(4) sin60° = (1)/(4) × (√3)/(2) = (√3)/(8)
Therefore L.H.S = (√3)/(8) × (√3)/(2) = (3)/(16)
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q5(iii). Prove that: sin10° sin30° sin50° sin70° = (1)/(16)

Ans: Method: use sin30° = (1)/(2), then product-to-sum identities on sin50° sin70°.
L.H.S = sin10° sin30° sin50° sin70°
= (1)/(2) × sin10° sin50° sin70° [since sin30° = (1)/(2)]
First find sin50° sin70° = (1)/(2)[cos(50° − 70°) − cos(50° + 70°)] [by sin α sin β identity]
= (1)/(2)[cos20° − cos120°] [since cos(−20°) = cos20°]
= (1)/(2)[cos20° + (1)/(2)] [since cos120° = −(1)/(2)]
Multiply by sin10°: sin10° sin50° sin70° = (1)/(2) sin10° cos20° + (1)/(4) sin10°
Now 2 sin10° cos20° = sin(10° + 20°) + sin(10° − 20°) = sin30° − sin10° [by 2 sin α cos β identity]
So sin10° sin50° sin70° = (1)/(4)(sin30° − sin10°) + (1)/(4) sin10° = (1)/(4) sin30° = (1)/(4) × (1)/(2) = (1)/(8)
Therefore L.H.S = (1)/(2) × (1)/(8) = (1)/(16)
= R.H.S
Hence proved.
