lessons.title: Exercise 11.4
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • For sides 3, 5, 6: S = 7, Δ = √56 ≈ 7.48, r = (Δ)/(S) ≈ 1.07 and R = (abc)/(4Δ) ≈ 3.01.
  • For sides 21, 20, 29: S = 35, Δ = 210, r = 6 and R = 14.5 exactly.
  • For sides 55 m, 25 m, 70 m: S = 75, Δ ≈ 612.37 m², r ≈ 8.16 m and the in-circle area πr² ≈ 209.44 m².
  • Escribed radius opposite side x is (Δ)/(S − x): for sides 20, 25, 30 dm, opposite 30 dm it is ≈ 33.07 dm and opposite 20 dm it is ≈ 14.17 dm.
  • Identities proved in the exercise: √(r r₁ r₂ r₃) = Δ, r₁r₂r₃ = rS², and (1)/(r₁) + (1)/(r₂) + (1)/(r₃) = (1)/(r).
  • Identity proved in the exercise: r₁ + r₂ + r₃ − r = 4R.
  • Escribed radii in half-angle form: r₁ = S tan(α/2), r₂ = S tan(β/2), r₃ = S tan(γ/2).
  • Sides in ratio 3 : 7 : 8 with r = 2 m give k = √3 and sides 3√3 ≈ 5.20 m, 7√3 ≈ 12.12 m, 8√3 ≈ 13.86 m.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Compute the in-radius r and circum-radius R of the triangle with sides: 3, 5, 6

Ans: Formulas used: Δ = √(S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c)) (Heron), r = (Δ)/(S), R = (abc)/(4Δ), where S = (1)/(2)(a + b + c).
Diagram (in words): The triangle has sides a = 3, b = 5 and c = 6. Its inscribed circle (in-circle) has radius r and its circumscribed circle (circum-circle) has radius R; both are to be computed.
Step 1: S = (1)/(2)(3 + 5 + 6) = 7
Step 2: Δ = √(7 × (7 − 3) × (7 − 5) × (7 − 6)) = √(7 × 4 × 2 × 1) = √56 ≈ 7.48
Step 3: r = (Δ)/(S) = (7.48)/(7) ≈ 1.07
Step 4: R = (abc)/(4Δ) = (3 × 5 × 6)/(4 × 7.48) = (90)/(29.93) ≈ 3.01
Answer: r ≈ 1.07, R ≈ 3.01 (the book's key gives R = 3.0, r = 1.07)

Q: Q1(ii). Compute the in-radius r and circum-radius R of the triangle with sides: 21, 20, 29

Ans: Formulas used: Δ = √(S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c)) (Heron), r = (Δ)/(S), R = (abc)/(4Δ), where S = (1)/(2)(a + b + c).
Diagram (in words): The triangle has sides a = 21, b = 20 and c = 29. Its inscribed circle (in-circle) has radius r and its circumscribed circle (circum-circle) has radius R; both are to be computed.
Step 1: S = (1)/(2)(21 + 20 + 29) = 35
Step 2: Δ = √(35 × (35 − 21) × (35 − 20) × (35 − 29)) = √(35 × 14 × 15 × 6) = √44100 = 210
Step 3: r = (Δ)/(S) = (210)/(35) = 6
Step 4: R = (abc)/(4Δ) = (21 × 20 × 29)/(4 × 210) = (12180)/(840) = 14.5
Answer: r = 6, R = 14.5

Q: Q2. Find the area of the inscribed circle of a triangle with sides 55 m, 25 m and 70 m.

Ans: Formulas used: Δ = √(S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c)) (Heron), in-radius r = (Δ)/(S), and area of the in-circle = πr².
Diagram (in words): The triangle has sides 55 m, 25 m and 70 m. A circle is inscribed in it, touching all three sides; its radius is r and its area is to be found.
Step 1: S = (1)/(2)(55 + 25 + 70) = (150)/(2) = 75
Step 2: Δ = √(75 × (75 − 55) × (75 − 25) × (75 − 70)) = √(75 × 20 × 50 × 5) = √375000 ≈ 612.37 m²
Step 3: r = (Δ)/(S) = (612.37)/(75) ≈ 8.16 m
Step 4: area of the inscribed circle = πr² = π × (8.165)² ≈ 3.1416 × 66.67 ≈ 209.44 m²
Answer: The area of the inscribed circle is ≈ 209 m²

Q: Q3(i). The sides of a triangle are 20, 25 and 30 decimeter. Find the radius of the described (escribed) circle opposite to the larger side.

Ans: Formulas used: Δ = √(S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c)) (Heron), and the escribed radius opposite a side x is Δ/(S − x).
Diagram (in words): The triangle has sides 20, 25 and 30 decimeter. The escribed circle opposite the larger side (30 dm) touches that side and the extensions of the other two sides; its radius is to be found.
Step 1: S = (1)/(2)(20 + 25 + 30) = (75)/(2) = 37.5
Step 2: Δ = √(37.5 × (37.5 − 20) × (37.5 − 25) × (37.5 − 30)) = √(37.5 × 17.5 × 12.5 × 7.5) = √61523.44 ≈ 248.04
Step 3: radius opposite the larger side 30 = (Δ)/(S − 30) = (248.04)/(37.5 − 30) = (248.04)/(7.5) ≈ 33.07
Answer: The radius of the escribed circle opposite the larger side is ≈ 33.07 dm

Q: Q3(ii). The sides of a triangle are 20, 25 and 30 decimeter. Find the radius of the described (escribed) circle opposite to the smaller side.

Ans: Formulas used: Δ = √(S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c)) (Heron), and the escribed radius opposite a side x is Δ/(S − x).
Diagram (in words): The triangle has sides 20, 25 and 30 decimeter. The escribed circle opposite the smaller side (20 dm) touches that side and the extensions of the other two sides; its radius is to be found.
Step 1: S = (1)/(2)(20 + 25 + 30) = (75)/(2) = 37.5
Step 2: Δ = √(37.5 × 17.5 × 12.5 × 7.5) ≈ 248.04 [as computed in part (i)]
Step 3: radius opposite the smaller side 20 = (Δ)/(S − 20) = (248.04)/(37.5 − 20) = (248.04)/(17.5) ≈ 14.17
Answer: The radius of the escribed circle opposite the smaller side is ≈ 14.17 dm

Q: Q4(i). Show that: √(r r₁ r₂ r₃) = Δ

Ans: Formulas used: r = (Δ)/(S), r₁ = (Δ)/(S − a), r₂ = (Δ)/(S − b), r₃ = (Δ)/(S − c), and Heron's relation Δ² = S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c).
r r₁ r₂ r₃ = ((Δ)/(S)) × ((Δ)/(S − a)) × ((Δ)/(S − b)) × ((Δ)/(S − c)) [substituting the four formulas]
= (Δ⁴)/(S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c))
= (Δ⁴)/(Δ²) [using Δ² = S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c)]
= Δ²
Taking the square root of both sides: √(r r₁ r₂ r₃) = Δ
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(ii). Show that: abc(sin α + sin β + sin γ) = 4ΔS

Ans: Formulas used: the sine law in the form sin α = (a)/(2R), sin β = (b)/(2R), sin γ = (c)/(2R), and R = (abc)/(4Δ), with 2S = a + b + c.
L.H.S = abc(sin α + sin β + sin γ)
= abc × ((a)/(2R) + (b)/(2R) + (c)/(2R)) [substituting the sine-law forms]
= (abc)/(2R) × (a + b + c) [taking out the common factor]
= (abc)/(2R) × 2S [since a + b + c = 2S]
= (abc × S)/(R)
Now substitute R = (abc)/(4Δ), i.e. (1)/(R) = (4Δ)/(abc):
L.H.S = abc × S × (4Δ)/(abc)
= 4ΔS [cancelling abc]
= R.H.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(iii). Show that: r₁r₂r₃ = rS²

Ans: Formulas used: r₁ = (Δ)/(S − a), r₂ = (Δ)/(S − b), r₃ = (Δ)/(S − c), r = (Δ)/(S), and Δ² = S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c).
r₁r₂r₃ = (Δ³)/((S − a)(S − b)(S − c)) [multiplying the three escribed radii]
From Δ² = S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c), we get (S − a)(S − b)(S − c) = (Δ²)/(S)
So r₁r₂r₃ = (Δ³)/((Δ²)/(S)) = ΔS
Also rS² = ((Δ)/(S)) × S² = ΔS
Hence r₁r₂r₃ = ΔS = rS²
Hence proved.

Q: Q5(i). Prove that for any ΔABC: r₁ + r₂ + r₃ − r = 4R

Ans: Formulas used: r₁ = (Δ)/(S − a), r₂ = (Δ)/(S − b), r₃ = (Δ)/(S − c), r = (Δ)/(S), Δ² = S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c) and R = (abc)/(4Δ).
Put x = S − a, y = S − b, z = S − c. Then S = x + y + z, and a = y + z, b = z + x, c = x + y.
r₁ + r₂ + r₃ − r = Δ((1)/(x) + (1)/(y) + (1)/(z) − (1)/(S))
= Δ × ((S(xy + yz + zx) − xyz)/(Sxyz)) [taking the common denominator Sxyz, with S = x + y + z]
Now Δ² = S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c) = Sxyz, so the denominator Sxyz = Δ².
Also (x + y + z)(xy + yz + zx) − xyz = (y + z)(z + x)(x + y) = abc [standard expansion]
So r₁ + r₂ + r₃ − r = Δ × (abc)/(Δ²) = (abc)/(Δ)
= 4R [since R = (abc)/(4Δ), so (abc)/(Δ) = 4R]
Hence proved.

Q: Q5(ii). Prove that for any ΔABC: r₁r₂ + r₂r₃ + r₃r₁ = S²

Ans: Formulas used: r₁ = (Δ)/(S − a) etc., and Δ² = S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c).
r₁r₂ = (Δ²)/((S − a)(S − b))
Since Δ² = S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c), we have (Δ²)/((S − a)(S − b)) = S(S − c)
So r₁r₂ = S(S − c)
Similarly r₂r₃ = S(S − a) and r₃r₁ = S(S − b)
Adding: r₁r₂ + r₂r₃ + r₃r₁ = S[(S − a) + (S − b) + (S − c)]
= S[3S − (a + b + c)]
= S[3S − 2S] [since a + b + c = 2S]
= S × S = S²
Hence proved.

Q: Q5(iii). Prove that for any ΔABC: (1)/(r₁) + (1)/(r₂) + (1)/(r₃) = (1)/(r)

Ans: Formulas used: (1)/(r₁) = (S − a)/(Δ), (1)/(r₂) = (S − b)/(Δ), (1)/(r₃) = (S − c)/(Δ), and (1)/(r) = (S)/(Δ).
(1)/(r₁) + (1)/(r₂) + (1)/(r₃) = ((S − a) + (S − b) + (S − c))/(Δ) [substituting and adding]
= (3S − (a + b + c))/(Δ)
= (3S − 2S)/(Δ) [since a + b + c = 2S]
= (S)/(Δ)
= (1)/(r) [since r = (Δ)/(S)]
Hence proved.

Q: Q6(i). Show that: r₁ = S tan(α/2) (the book prints the semi-perimeter as s in this question)

Ans: Formulas used: tan(α/2) = (r)/(S − a) (half-angle tangent formula), r₁ = (Δ)/(S − a) and Δ = rS.
The half-angle formula gives tan(α/2) = √((S − b)(S − c)/(S(S − a))) and r = √((S − a)(S − b)(S − c)/(S)), so dividing, tan(α/2) = (r)/(S − a).
Hence r = (S − a) tan(α/2) ... (1)
Now r₁ = (Δ)/(S − a) [escribed radius formula]
= (rS)/(S − a) [using Δ = rS]
= S × (r)/((S − a))
= S tan(α/2) [using (1): (r)/((S − a)) = tan(α/2)]
Hence r₁ = S tan(α/2).
Hence proved.

Q: Q6(ii). Show that: r₂ = S tan(β/2) (the book prints the semi-perimeter as s in this question)

Ans: Formulas used: tan(β/2) = (r)/(S − b) (half-angle tangent formula), r₂ = (Δ)/(S − b) and Δ = rS.
The half-angle formula gives tan(β/2) = √((S − a)(S − c)/(S(S − b))) and r = √((S − a)(S − b)(S − c)/(S)), so dividing, tan(β/2) = (r)/(S − b).
Hence r = (S − b) tan(β/2) ... (1)
Now r₂ = (Δ)/(S − b) [escribed radius formula]
= (rS)/(S − b) [using Δ = rS]
= S × (r)/((S − b))
= S tan(β/2) [using (1): (r)/((S − b)) = tan(β/2)]
Hence r₂ = S tan(β/2).
Hence proved.

Q: Q6(iii). Show that: r₃ = S tan(γ/2) (the book prints the semi-perimeter as s in this question)

Ans: Formulas used: tan(γ/2) = (r)/(S − c) (half-angle tangent formula), r₃ = (Δ)/(S − c) and Δ = rS.
The half-angle formula gives tan(γ/2) = √((S − a)(S − b)/(S(S − c))) and r = √((S − a)(S − b)(S − c)/(S)), so dividing, tan(γ/2) = (r)/(S − c).
Hence r = (S − c) tan(γ/2) ... (1)
Now r₃ = (Δ)/(S − c) [escribed radius formula]
= (rS)/(S − c) [using Δ = rS]
= S × (r)/((S − c))
= S tan(γ/2) [using (1): (r)/((S − c)) = tan(γ/2)]
Hence r₃ = S tan(γ/2).
Hence proved.

Q: Q7. The sides of a triangle are in the ratio 3 : 7 : 8 and the radius of the inscribed circle is 2 m. Find the sides of the triangle.

Ans: Formulas used: Heron's formula Δ = √(S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c)) and r = (Δ)/(S).
Diagram (in words): The triangle has sides in the ratio 3 : 7 : 8, so its sides can be written as 3k, 7k and 8k for some positive number k. Its inscribed circle has radius r = 2 m. We have to find k and hence the three sides.
Step 1: let the sides be a = 3k, b = 7k, c = 8k
Step 2: S = (1)/(2)(3k + 7k + 8k) = 9k
Step 3: S − a = 6k, S − b = 2k, S − c = k
Step 4: Δ = √(9k × 6k × 2k × k) = √(108k⁴) = 6√3 k²
Step 5: r = (Δ)/(S) = (6√3 k²)/(9k) = (2√3)/(3) k
Step 6: given r = 2, so (2√3)/(3) k = 2, giving k = (3)/(√3) = √3
Step 7: sides are 3k = 3√3 ≈ 5.20 m, 7k = 7√3 ≈ 12.12 m, 8k = 8√3 ≈ 13.86 m
Answer: The sides are 3√3 m ≈ 5.20 m, 7√3 m ≈ 12.12 m and 8√3 m ≈ 13.86 m

mcqs.q: For sides 3, 5, 6, what is the in-radius r?
For sides 3, 5, 6, what is the circum-radius R?
For sides 21, 20, 29, what are r and R?
For sides 55 m, 25 m, 70 m, what is the area of the inscribed circle?
For sides 20, 25, 30 dm, what is the escribed radius opposite the larger side 30 dm?
For sides 20, 25, 30 dm, what is the escribed radius opposite the smaller side 20 dm?
Which identity is proved for r, r₁, r₂, r₃ and Δ?
mcqs.why: Product: r r₁ r₂ r₃ = (Δ⁴)/(S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c)) = (Δ⁴)/(Δ²) = Δ², using Δ² = S(S − a)(S − b)(S − c). Taking square roots gives √(r r₁ r₂ r₃) = Δ.

mcqs.q: Which identity relates r₁ + r₂ + r₃ − r to R?
mcqs.why: The proof gives r₁ + r₂ + r₃ − r = (abc)/(Δ). Since R = (abc)/(4Δ), (abc)/(Δ) = 4R. Hence r₁ + r₂ + r₃ − r = 4R.

mcqs.q: What is r₁ in terms of S and α?
mcqs.why: From tan(α/2) = (r)/(S − a), r = (S − a) tan(α/2). Then r₁ = (Δ)/(S − a) = (rS)/(S − a) = S tan(α/2). Hence r₁ = S tan(α/2).

mcqs.q: Sides are in ratio 3 : 7 : 8 and r = 2 m. What is the largest side?
mcqs.why: Let sides be 3k, 7k, 8k. S = 9k, Δ = √(9k × 6k × 2k × k) = 6√3 k². r = (Δ)/(S) = (2√3)/(3)k = 2 gives k = √3. Largest side = 8k = 8√3 ≈ 13.86 m.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 11
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Right-triangle Pythagoras: with a = 2, c = 5, γ = 90°, b = √(25 − 4) = √21.
  • An escalator at 45° rising 24 ft has length (24)/(sin45°) = 24√2 ft.
  • Heron check: for sides 3, 5, 6, S = 7 and Δ = √(7(4)(2)(1)).
  • Angle of depression 30° from a 75 m tower gives object distance (75)/(tan30°) = 75√3 m.
  • The perpendicular bisectors of a triangle meet at the circumcentre, and r r₁ r₂ r₃ = Δ².
  • SAS review case a = 15.6, b = 18, γ = 35°10′ gives c ≈ 10.40, α ≈ 59°43′, β ≈ 85°07′.
  • No triangle exists with sides 34, 23, 58 because 34 + 23 = 57 < 58.
  • A building seen at 48° from A and 61° from B with AB = 20 m has height ≈ 57.79 m.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). In a right triangle ABC, if a = 2, c = 5 and γ = 90°, then b = ?

Options: (a) 7 (b) 3 (c) √21 (d) √29

Correct answer: √21

Q: Q1(ii). An escalator in a department store makes an angle of 45° with the ground. If it carries people a vertical distance of 24 feet, then the length of the escalator is:

Options: (a) 12√2 ft (b) 24√2 ft (c) 8√3 ft (d) 48 ft

Correct answer: 24√2 ft

Q: Q1(iii). The area of an isosceles triangle whose base is a and one of the equal sides is b is:

Options: (a) (a)/(4) √(4b² − a²) (b) (b)/(4) √(4b² − a²) (c) ((a + b))/(4) √(a² − b²) (d) ((a − b))/(4) √(b² − a²)

Correct answer: (a)/(4) √(4b² − a²)

Q: Q1(iv). For a = 3 m, b = 5 m, c = 6 m, by Heron's formula Δ = ?

Options: (a) Δ = 7√((10)(12)(13)) (b) Δ = √((4)(2)(1)) (c) Δ = √(7(3)(5)(6)) (d) Δ = √(7(4)(2)(1))

Correct answer: Δ = √(7(4)(2)(1))

Q: Q1(v). In the figure, ΔABC is right-angled at B, ∠A = 30°, the hypotenuse AC = 6 cm; then BC = ?

Options: (a) 2√3 cm (b) 3√3 cm (c) 4√3 cm (d) 3 cm

Correct answer: 3 cm

Q: Q1(vi). If the angle of depression of an object from a 75 m high tower is 30°, then the distance of the object from the tower is:

Options: (a) 25√3 m (b) 50√3 m (c) 75√3 m (d) 150 m

Correct answer: 75√3 m

Q: Q1(vii). The point of concurrency of the right bisectors of the sides of a triangle is called:

Options: (a) In-Centre (b) Orthocenter (c) Circumcentre (d) Centroid

Correct answer: Circumcentre

Q: Q1(viii). With usual notations, r r₁ r₂ r₃ = ?

Options: (a) Δ (b) Δ² (c) (abc)/(Δ) (d) (Δ)/(abc)

Correct answer: Δ²

Q: Q2(i). Solve the triangle: a = 0.7, c = 0.8, β = 141°30′

Ans: Method: two sides and the included angle are given (SAS), so find b by the cosine law, then an angle by the sine law.
Diagram (in words): ΔABC has the standard notation: side a = BC = 0.7 opposite α, side c = AB = 0.8 opposite γ, and the included angle between them at B is β = 141°30′. Side b = CA opposite β is unknown. We have to find b, α and γ.
Step 1 (cosine law): b² = a² + c² − 2ac cos β = 0.7² + 0.8² − 2(0.7)(0.8) cos141°30′
= 0.49 + 0.64 − 1.12 × (−0.78261) = 1.13 + 0.87652 = 2.00652
So b = √2.00652 ≈ 1.42
Step 2 (sine law): sin α = (a sin β)/(b) = (0.7 × sin141°30′)/(1.42) = (0.7 × 0.62251)/(1.42) = 0.30762
So α = sin⁻¹(0.30762) ≈ 17°55′
Step 3: γ = 180° − β − α ≈ 180° − 141°30′ − 17°55′ = 20°35′
Answer: b ≈ 1.42, α ≈ 17°55′, γ ≈ 20°35′
Note: The book's printed answers (α = 17.2°, γ = 21.3°) are incorrect; the correct answers are α ≈ 17°55′ (17.9°) and γ ≈ 20°35′ (20.6°). The printed value b = 1.42 is correct.

Q: Q2(ii). Solve the triangle: a = 34, b = 23, c = 58

Ans: Method: check the triangle inequality first: in any triangle, the sum of any two sides must exceed the third side.
Diagram (in words): ΔABC would have sides a = BC = 34, b = CA = 23 and c = AB = 58. Before solving, the three lengths must be able to form a triangle.
Step 1: add the two shorter sides: a + b = 34 + 23 = 57
Step 2: compare with the longest side: 57 < 58 = c
Step 3: since a + b < c, the two shorter sides cannot meet, and no such triangle exists.
Answer: No triangle is possible with sides 34, 23 and 58 (the book's answer key also gives: No triangle possible)

Q: Q2(iii). Solve the triangle: a = 15.6, b = 18, γ = 35°10′

Ans: Method: two sides and the included angle are given (SAS), so find c by the cosine law, then an angle by the sine law.
Diagram (in words): ΔABC has the standard notation: side a = BC = 15.6 opposite α, side b = CA = 18 opposite β, and the included angle between them at C is γ = 35°10′. Side c = AB opposite γ is unknown. We have to find c, α and β.
Step 1 (cosine law): c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos γ = 15.6² + 18² − 2(15.6)(18) cos35°10′
= 243.36 + 324 − 561.6 × 0.81714 = 567.36 − 458.87 = 108.49
So c = √108.49 ≈ 10.40
Step 2 (sine law): sin α = (a sin γ)/(c) = (15.6 × sin35°10′)/(10.40) = (15.6 × 0.57601)/(10.40) = 0.86268
So α = sin⁻¹(0.86268) ≈ 59°43′
Step 3: β = 180° − γ − α ≈ 180° − 35°10′ − 59°43′ = 85°07′
Answer: c ≈ 10.40, α ≈ 59°43′, β ≈ 85°07′

Q: Q2(iv). Solve the triangle: a = 48, b = 32, γ = 57°

Ans: Method: two sides and the included angle are given (SAS), so find c by the cosine law, then an angle by the sine law.
Diagram (in words): ΔABC has the standard notation: side a = BC = 48 opposite α, side b = CA = 32 opposite β, and the included angle between them at C is γ = 57°. Side c = AB opposite γ is unknown. We have to find c, α and β.
Step 1 (cosine law): c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos γ = 48² + 32² − 2(48)(32) cos57°
= 2304 + 1024 − 3072 × 0.54464 = 3328 − 1673.13 = 1654.87
So c = √1654.87 ≈ 40.68
Step 2 (sine law): sin α = (a sin γ)/(c) = (48 × sin57°)/(40.68) = (48 × 0.83867)/(40.68) = 0.98981
So α = sin⁻¹(0.98981) ≈ 81°43′
Step 3: β = 180° − γ − α ≈ 180° − 57° − 81°43′ = 41°17′
Answer: c ≈ 40.68, α ≈ 81°43′, β ≈ 41°17′

Q: Q2(v). Solve the triangle: b = 35, c = 37, α = 23°25′

Ans: Method: two sides and the included angle are given (SAS), so find a by the cosine law, then an angle by the sine law.
Diagram (in words): ΔABC has the standard notation: side b = CA = 35 opposite β, side c = AB = 37 opposite γ, and the included angle between them at A is α = 23°25′. Side a = BC opposite α is unknown. We have to find a, β and γ.
Step 1 (cosine law): a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos α = 35² + 37² − 2(35)(37) cos23°25′
= 1225 + 1369 − 2590 × 0.91765 = 2594 − 2376.71 = 217.29
So a = √217.29 ≈ 14.74
Step 2 (sine law): sin β = (b sin α)/(a) = (35 × sin23°25′)/(14.74) = (35 × 0.39715)/(14.74) = 0.94306
So β = sin⁻¹(0.94306) ≈ 70°39′
Step 3: γ = 180° − α − β ≈ 180° − 23°25′ − 70°39′ = 85°56′
Answer: a ≈ 14.74, β ≈ 70°39′, γ ≈ 85°56′

Q: Q2(vi). Solve the triangle: a = 58.4, β = 37.2°, γ = 100°

Ans: Method: two angles and a side are given, so find the third angle and use the sine law for the remaining sides.
Diagram (in words): ΔABC has the standard notation: side a = BC = 58.4 opposite the unknown angle α at A, with angles β = 37.2° at B and γ = 100° at C given. We have to find α and sides b = CA and c = AB.
Step 1: α = 180° − β − γ = 180° − 37.2° − 100° = 42.8°
Step 2 (sine law): b = (a sin β)/(sin α) = (58.4 × sin37.2°)/(sin42.8°) = (58.4 × 0.60449)/(0.67944) ≈ 51.97
Step 3 (sine law): c = (a sin γ)/(sin α) = (58.4 × sin100°)/(sin42.8°) = (58.4 × 0.98481)/(0.67944) ≈ 84.65
Answer: α = 42.8°, b ≈ 51.97, c ≈ 84.65

Q: Q2(vii). Solve the triangle: c = 13.6, α = 30°24′, β = 72°6′

Ans: Method: two angles and a side are given, so find the third angle and use the sine law for the remaining sides.
Diagram (in words): ΔABC has the standard notation: side c = AB = 13.6 opposite the unknown angle γ at C, with angles α = 30°24′ at A and β = 72°6′ at B given. We have to find γ and sides a = BC and b = CA.
Step 1: γ = 180° − α − β = 180° − 30°24′ − 72°6′ = 77°30′
Step 2 (sine law): a = (c sin α)/(sin γ) = (13.6 × sin30°24′)/(sin77°30′) = (13.6 × 0.50599)/(0.97654) ≈ 7.05
Step 3 (sine law): b = (c sin β)/(sin γ) = (13.6 × sin72°6′)/(sin77°30′) = (13.6 × 0.95182)/(0.97654) ≈ 13.26
Answer: γ = 77°30′, a ≈ 7.05, b ≈ 13.26

Q: Q3(i). Find the measure of the smallest angle of the triangle whose sides have lengths: 4.3, 5.1 and 6.3

Ans: Method: the smallest angle is opposite the smallest side; use the cosine law.
Diagram (in words): The triangle has sides 4.3, 5.1 and 6.3. The smallest angle, call it α, is opposite the shortest side 4.3, with the sides 5.1 and 6.3 on either side of it. We have to find α.
Step 1 (cosine law): cos α = (5.1² + 6.3² − 4.3²)/(2 × 5.1 × 6.3)
Step 2: cos α = (26.01 + 39.69 − 18.49)/(64.26) = (47.21)/(64.26) ≈ 0.73471
Step 3: α = cos⁻¹(0.73471) ≈ 42°43′
Answer: The smallest angle is ≈ 42°43′ (42.7°)

Q: Q3(ii). Find the measure of the smallest angle of the triangle whose sides have lengths: 3, 4.2 and 3.8

Ans: Method: the smallest angle is opposite the smallest side; use the cosine law.
Diagram (in words): The triangle has sides 3, 4.2 and 3.8. The smallest angle, call it α, is opposite the shortest side 3, with the sides 4.2 and 3.8 on either side of it. We have to find α.
Step 1 (cosine law): cos α = (4.2² + 3.8² − 3²)/(2 × 4.2 × 3.8)
Step 2: cos α = (17.64 + 14.44 − 9)/(31.92) = (23.08)/(31.92) ≈ 0.72306
Step 3: α = cos⁻¹(0.72306) ≈ 43°42′
Answer: The smallest angle is ≈ 43°42′ (43.7°)

Q: Q4(i). Find the measure of the largest angle of the triangle whose sides have lengths: 2.9, 3.3 and 4.1

Ans: Method: the largest angle is opposite the largest side; use the cosine law.
Diagram (in words): The triangle has sides 2.9, 3.3 and 4.1. The largest angle, call it γ, is opposite the longest side 4.1, with the sides 2.9 and 3.3 on either side of it. We have to find γ.
Step 1 (cosine law): cos γ = (2.9² + 3.3² − 4.1²)/(2 × 2.9 × 3.3)
Step 2: cos γ = (8.41 + 10.89 − 16.81)/(19.14) = (2.49)/(19.14) ≈ 0.13009
Step 3: γ = cos⁻¹(0.13009) ≈ 82°31′
Answer: The largest angle is ≈ 82°31′ (82.5°)

Q: Q4(ii). Find the measure of the largest angle of the triangle whose sides have lengths: 6.0, 8 and 9.4

Ans: Method: the largest angle is opposite the largest side; use the cosine law.
Diagram (in words): The triangle has sides 6.0, 8 and 9.4. The largest angle, call it γ, is opposite the longest side 9.4, with the sides 6.0 and 8 on either side of it. We have to find γ.
Step 1 (cosine law): cos γ = (6.0² + 8² − 9.4²)/(2 × 6.0 × 8)
Step 2: cos γ = (36 + 64 − 88.36)/(96) = (11.64)/(96) ≈ 0.12125
Step 3: γ = cos⁻¹(0.12125) ≈ 83°02′
Answer: The largest angle is ≈ 83°02′ (83.03°)

Q: Q5. The sides of a parallelogram are 25 cm and 35 cm long and one of its angles is 36°. Find the lengths of its diagonals.

Ans: Method: each diagonal forms a triangle with the two sides; the diagonal opposite the 36° angle uses the cosine law with 36°, and the other diagonal uses the supplementary angle 180° − 36° = 144°.
Diagram (in words): The parallelogram has adjacent sides 25 cm and 35 cm, with an angle of 36° between them at one vertex. One diagonal joins the ends of these sides across the 36° angle's supplement, and the other diagonal spans the 36° angle's opposite corner; the two diagonals are found from the two triangles with included angles 144° and 36° respectively. We have to find both diagonal lengths.
Step 1: the diagonal across the angle 144° (the longer diagonal): p² = 25² + 35² − 2(25)(35) cos144°
= 625 + 1225 − 1750 × (−0.80902) = 1850 + 1415.78 = 3265.78
So p = √3265.78 ≈ 57.15 cm
Step 2: the diagonal across the angle 36° (the shorter diagonal): q² = 25² + 35² − 2(25)(35) cos36°
= 1850 − 1750 × 0.80902 = 1850 − 1415.78 = 434.22
So q = √434.22 ≈ 20.84 cm
Answer: The diagonals are ≈ 57.15 cm and ≈ 20.84 cm

Q: Q6. A man is flying a kite. He has let out 50 m of string, and he notices that the string makes an angle of 60° with the ground. How high is the kite? (Figure: the string runs from the man's hand at S on the ground up to the kite K, and P is the point on the ground directly below the kite.)

Ans: Method: the string is the hypotenuse of a right triangle; use sin60° = (height)/(string length).
Diagram (in words): S is the point on the ground where the man holds the string, K is the kite, and P is the point on the ground directly below the kite, so KP is the vertical height of the kite and SP is horizontal. The string SK = 50 m makes an angle of 60° with the ground at S. Triangle SKP is right-angled at P. We have to find KP.
Step 1: in ΔSKP, sin60° = (KP)/(SK) = (KP)/(50)
Step 2: KP = 50 × sin60° = 50 × (√3)/(2)
Step 3: KP = 25√3 ≈ 43.30 m
Answer: The kite is 25√3 m ≈ 43.30 m high

Q: Q7. A robin on a branch 40 ft up in a tree spots a worm at an angle of depression of 14°. From a branch 15 ft above the robin, a crow spots the same worm at an angle of depression of 19°. How far is each bird from the worm?

Ans: Method: for each bird, distance to the worm = (height of the bird)/(sin(angle of depression)), since the angle of depression equals the angle of elevation from the worm.
Diagram (in words): The tree is vertical. The worm W is on the ground at some horizontal distance from the foot of the tree. The robin R is 40 ft above the ground, and the crow C is 15 ft above the robin, i.e. 55 ft above the ground. The angle of depression of W from R is 14°, and from C is 19°. The straight-line distances RW and CW are to be found; each forms the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the bird's height as the opposite side.
Step 1 (robin): sin14° = (40)/(RW), so RW = (40)/(sin14°) = (40)/(0.24192) ≈ 165.34 ft
Step 2 (crow): the crow's height is 40 + 15 = 55 ft; sin19° = (55)/(CW), so CW = (55)/(sin19°) = (55)/(0.32557) ≈ 168.93 ft
Answer: The robin is ≈ 165.34 ft from the worm and the crow is ≈ 168.93 ft from the worm (the book's key prints only the crow's distance, 168.93 ft)

Q: Q8. The angle of elevation of a building is 48° from A and 61° from B. If AB is 20 m, find the height of the building.

Ans: Method: let the foot of the building be F and its height h; write FA and FB using cot of the angles of elevation and use FA − FB = AB = 20 m.
Diagram (in words): The building is vertical with foot F and top T, height h = TF to be found. Points A and B lie on the same horizontal line through F, with B nearer the building and A farther away, and AB = 20 m. The angle of elevation of T from A is 48° and from B is 61°. Triangles TFA and TFB are right-angled at F.
Step 1: in ΔTFB, tan61° = (h)/(FB), so FB = h cot61° = h × 0.55431
Step 2: in ΔTFA, tan48° = (h)/(FA), so FA = h cot48° = h × 0.90040
Step 3: FA − FB = AB = 20, so h(0.90040 − 0.55431) = 20
Step 4: h × 0.34610 = 20, so h = (20)/(0.34610) ≈ 57.79 m
Answer: The height of the building is ≈ 57.8 m

mcqs.q: In a right triangle ABC, if a = 2, c = 5 and γ = 90°, then b = ?
mcqs.why: Use Pythagoras: b² = c² − a² = 5² − 2² = 25 − 4 = 21. Then b = √21. So b = √21.

mcqs.q: An escalator makes an angle of 45° with the ground and carries people a vertical distance of 24 feet. What is the length of the escalator?
mcqs.why: Use sin45° = (vertical)/(length), so length = (24)/(sin45°) = (24)/((√2)/(2)) = 24√2 ft. So the length is 24√2 ft.

mcqs.q: The area of an isosceles triangle whose base is a and one of the equal sides is b is:
For a = 3 m, b = 5 m, c = 6 m, by Heron's formula Δ = ?
ΔABC is right-angled at B, ∠A = 30°, hypotenuse AC = 6 cm. Then BC = ?
mcqs.why: BC is opposite 30°. Use sin30° = (BC)/(AC), so BC = AC × sin30° = 6 × (1)/(2) = 3 cm. So BC = 3 cm.

mcqs.q: If the angle of depression of an object from a 75 m high tower is 30°, what is the distance of the object from the tower?
mcqs.why: Use tan30° = (75)/(distance), so distance = (75)/(tan30°) = (75)/((1)/(√3)) = 75√3 m. So the distance is 75√3 m.

mcqs.q: The point of concurrency of the right bisectors of the sides of a triangle is called:
mcqs.why: The perpendicular (right) bisectors of the sides meet at the circumcentre, the centre of the circumscribed circle equidistant from all three vertices.

mcqs.q: With usual notations, r r₁ r₂ r₃ = ?
mcqs.why: From Q4(i) of Exercise 11.4, √(r r₁ r₂ r₃) = Δ. Squaring both sides gives r r₁ r₂ r₃ = Δ². So the product equals Δ².

mcqs.q: Solve the triangle a = 15.6, b = 18, γ = 35°10′. What is c?
What is the smallest angle of a triangle with sides 4.3, 5.1 and 6.3?
What is the largest angle of a triangle with sides 2.9, 3.3 and 4.1?
A parallelogram has sides 25 cm and 35 cm with an angle of 36°. What is the longer diagonal?
A kite string is 50 m long and makes 60° with the ground. How high is the kite?
mcqs.why: Use sin60° = (height)/(50), so height = 50 × sin60° = 50 × (√3)/(2) = 25√3 ≈ 43.30 m. The kite is ≈ 43.30 m high.

mcqs.q: The angle of elevation of a building is 48° from A and 61° from B, with AB = 20 m. What is the height?
Can a triangle have sides a = 34, b = 23, c = 58?
mcqs.why: Check triangle inequality: a + b = 34 + 23 = 57, which is less than c = 58. Since the two shorter sides cannot meet, no triangle is possible.

chapters.title: Unit 12: Graph of Trigonometric and Inverse Trigonometric Functions and Solutions of Trigonometric Equations

lessons.title: Exercise 12.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Domain of 3 sin 3x is R and its range is [−3, 3]; its period is (2π)/(3).
  • tan (1)/(2) x is undefined when x = (2n + 1)π, n ∈ Z; its range is R and its period is 2π.
  • cosec 2x is undefined when x = (nπ)/(2); its range is R − (−1, 1) and its period is π.
  • cos 4x has domain R, range [−1, 1] and period (π)/(2).
  • 6 sec 2x is undefined when x = (2n + 1)(π)/(4); its range is R − (−6, 6) and its period is π.
  • (7)/(2) cot (2πx)/(3) has period (3)/(2) and is undefined when x = (3n)/(2).
  • For y = a + b sin(cθ + d), maximum = a + |b| and minimum = a − |b|.
  • y = −2 + (1)/(2) sin((1)/(3) θ + 2) has maximum −(3)/(2) and minimum −(5)/(2); y = 5 − 4 sin(θ + 30) has maximum 9 and minimum 1.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Find the domain, range and period of 3 sin 3x

Ans: Method: use the domain, range and period of sin t, with t = 3x.
Domain: sin t is defined for every real t.
So 3 sin 3x is defined for every real x.
Domain = R.
Range: for every t, −1 ≤ sin t ≤ 1.
Put t = 3x: −1 ≤ sin 3x ≤ 1.
Multiply by 3: −3 ≤ 3 sin 3x ≤ 3.
Range = [−3, 3].
Period: the period of sin x is 2π.
Period of sin 3x = (2π)/(3).
Multiplying by the constant 3 does not change the period.
Answer: Domain = R, Range = [−3, 3], Period = (2π)/(3).

Q: Q1(ii). Find the domain, range and period of tan (1)/(2) x

Ans: Method: use the domain, range and period of tan t, with t = (1)/(2) x.
Domain: tan t is defined for t ≠ (2n + 1)(π)/(2), n ∈ Z.
Put t = (1)/(2) x: (1)/(2) x ≠ (2n + 1)(π)/(2).
Multiply by 2: x ≠ (2n + 1)π, n ∈ Z.
Domain = R − {x | x = (2n + 1)π, n ∈ Z}.
Range: tan t takes every real value.
Range = R.
Period: the period of tan x is π.
Period of tan (1)/(2) x = (π)/((1)/(2)) = 2π.
Answer: Domain = R − {x | x = (2n + 1)π, n ∈ Z}, Range = R, Period = 2π.

Q: Q1(iii). Find the domain, range and period of cosec 2x

Ans: Method: use the domain, range and period of cosec t, with t = 2x.
Domain: cosec t is defined for t ≠ nπ, n ∈ Z.
Put t = 2x: 2x ≠ nπ.
Divide by 2: x ≠ (nπ)/(2), n ∈ Z.
Domain = R − {x | x = (nπ)/(2), n ∈ Z}.
Range: cosec t ≤ −1 or cosec t ≥ 1 for every t in its domain.
So cosec 2x ≤ −1 or cosec 2x ≥ 1.
Range = R − (−1, 1).
Period: the period of cosec x is 2π.
Period of cosec 2x = (2π)/(2) = π.
Answer: Domain = R − {x | x = (nπ)/(2), n ∈ Z}, Range = R − (−1, 1), Period = π.

Q: Q1(iv). Find the domain, range and period of cos 4x

Ans: Method: use the domain, range and period of cos t, with t = 4x.
Domain: cos t is defined for every real t.
Domain = R.
Range: for every t, −1 ≤ cos t ≤ 1.
Put t = 4x: −1 ≤ cos 4x ≤ 1.
Range = [−1, 1].
Period: the period of cos x is 2π.
Period of cos 4x = (2π)/(4) = (π)/(2).
Answer: Domain = R, Range = [−1, 1], Period = (π)/(2).

Q: Q1(v). Find the domain, range and period of 6 sec 2x

Ans: Method: use the domain, range and period of sec t, with t = 2x.
Domain: sec t is defined for t ≠ (2n + 1)(π)/(2), n ∈ Z.
Put t = 2x: 2x ≠ (2n + 1)(π)/(2).
Divide by 2: x ≠ (2n + 1)(π)/(4), n ∈ Z.
Domain = R − {x | x = (2n + 1)(π)/(4), n ∈ Z}.
Range: sec t ≤ −1 or sec t ≥ 1 for every t in its domain.
Multiply by 6: 6 sec 2x ≤ −6 or 6 sec 2x ≥ 6.
Range = R − (−6, 6).
Period: the period of sec x is 2π.
Period of sec 2x = (2π)/(2) = π.
Multiplying by the constant 6 does not change the period.
Answer: Domain = R − {x | x = (2n + 1)(π)/(4), n ∈ Z}, Range = R − (−6, 6), Period = π.

Q: Q1(vi). Find the domain, range and period of (7)/(2) cot (2πx)/(3)

Ans: Method: use the domain, range and period of cot t, with t = (2πx)/(3).
Domain: cot t is defined for t ≠ nπ, n ∈ Z.
Put t = (2πx)/(3): (2πx)/(3) ≠ nπ.
Multiply by (3)/(2π): x ≠ (3n)/(2), n ∈ Z.
Domain = R − {x | x = (3n)/(2), n ∈ Z}.
Range: cot t takes every real value, and so does (7)/(2) cot t.
Range = R.
Period: the period of cot x is π.
Period of cot (2πx)/(3) = (π)/((2π)/(3)) = (3)/(2).
Multiplying by the constant (7)/(2) does not change the period.
Answer: Domain = R − {x | x = (3n)/(2), n ∈ Z}, Range = R, Period = (3)/(2).

Q: Q1(vii). Find the domain, range and period of −(1)/(4) tan x

Ans: Method: use the domain, range and period of tan x.
Domain: tan x is defined for x ≠ (2n + 1)(π)/(2), n ∈ Z.
Domain = R − {x | x = (2n + 1)(π)/(2), n ∈ Z}.
Range: tan x takes every real value, and so does −(1)/(4) tan x.
Range = R.
Period: the period of tan x is π.
Multiplying by the constant −(1)/(4) does not change the period.
Period = π.
Answer: Domain = R − {x | x = (2n + 1)(π)/(2), n ∈ Z}, Range = R, Period = π.

Q: Q1(viii). Find the domain, range and period of (1)/(2) cosec x

Ans: Method: use the domain, range and period of cosec x.
Domain: cosec x is defined for x ≠ nπ, n ∈ Z.
Domain = R − {x | x = nπ, n ∈ Z}.
Range: cosec x ≤ −1 or cosec x ≥ 1.
Multiply by (1)/(2): (1)/(2) cosec x ≤ −(1)/(2) or (1)/(2) cosec x ≥ (1)/(2).
Range = R − (−(1)/(2), (1)/(2)).
Period: the period of cosec x is 2π.
Multiplying by the constant (1)/(2) does not change the period.
Period = 2π.
Answer: Domain = R − {x | x = nπ, n ∈ Z}, Range = R − (−(1)/(2), (1)/(2)), Period = 2π.

Q: Q1(ix). Find the domain, range and period of sec (π)/(4) x

Ans: Method: use the domain, range and period of sec t, with t = (π)/(4) x.
Domain: sec t is defined for t ≠ (2n + 1)(π)/(2), n ∈ Z.
Put t = (π)/(4) x: (π)/(4) x ≠ (2n + 1)(π)/(2).
Multiply by (4)/(π): x ≠ 2(2n + 1) = 4n + 2, n ∈ Z.
Domain = R − {x | x = 4n + 2, n ∈ Z}.
Range: sec t ≤ −1 or sec t ≥ 1 for every t in its domain.
Range = R − (−1, 1).
Period: the period of sec x is 2π.
Period of sec (π)/(4) x = (2π)/((π)/(4)) = 8.
Answer: Domain = R − {x | x = 4n + 2, n ∈ Z}, Range = R − (−1, 1), Period = 8.

Q: Q2(i). Find maximum and minimum of y = −2 + (1)/(2) sin((1)/(3) θ + 2)

Ans: Method: for y = a + b sin(cθ + d), maximum = a + |b| and minimum = a − |b|.
Here a = −2 and b = (1)/(2).
The values of c and d do not affect the maximum and minimum.
Maximum value = a + |b|
= −2 + |(1)/(2)|
= −2 + (1)/(2)
= −(3)/(2).
Minimum value = a − |b|
= −2 − |(1)/(2)|
= −2 − (1)/(2)
= −(5)/(2).
Answer: Maximum = −(3)/(2), Minimum = −(5)/(2).

Q: Q2(ii). Find maximum and minimum of y = 5 − 4 sin(θ + 30)

Ans: Method: for y = a + b sin(cθ + d), maximum = a + |b| and minimum = a − |b|.
Here a = 5 and b = −4.
Maximum value = a + |b|
= 5 + |−4|
= 5 + 4
= 9.
Minimum value = a − |b|
= 5 − |−4|
= 5 − 4
= 1.
Answer: Maximum = 9, Minimum = 1.

Q: Q2(iii). Find maximum and minimum of y = (1)/(19 − 10 sin(3θ − 45))

Ans: Method: first find the maximum and minimum of the denominator, then take reciprocals.
Let y′ = 19 − 10 sin(3θ − 45), so y = (1)/(y′).
For y′: a = 19 and b = −10.
Maximum of y′ = a + |b| = 19 + 10 = 29.
Minimum of y′ = a − |b| = 19 − 10 = 9.
So 9 ≤ y′ ≤ 29; in particular y′ is always positive and never zero.
The reciprocal is largest when the denominator is smallest.
Maximum value of y = (1)/(9).
The reciprocal is smallest when the denominator is largest.
Minimum value of y = (1)/(29).
Answer: Maximum = (1)/(9), Minimum = (1)/(29).

Q: Q2(iv). Find maximum and minimum of y = (1)/(4 cos 2πθ)

Ans: Method: write the function as a reciprocal, y = (1)/(4) sec 2πθ, and use the range of sec.
cos 2πθ takes every value from −1 to 1.
So 4 cos 2πθ takes every value from −4 to 4, except 0, where y is not defined.
On the positive side, 4 cos 2πθ is largest, namely 4, when cos 2πθ = 1.
There y = (1)/(4), and this is the smallest positive value of y.
On the negative side, 4 cos 2πθ is smallest, namely −4, when cos 2πθ = −1.
There y = −(1)/(4), and this is the largest negative value of y.
As cos 2πθ approaches 0, |y| grows without bound, so y has no maximum and no minimum value.
Answer: y has no maximum or minimum; its smallest positive value is (1)/(4) and its largest negative value is −(1)/(4), the values given in the book's answer key.

mcqs.q: What is the period of 3 sin 3x?
mcqs.why: Period rule: period of sin(bx) = (2π)/(|b|). Here b = 3, so period = (2π)/(3). The outside factor 3 changes amplitude only, not period.

mcqs.q: What is the range of 3 sin 3x?
mcqs.why: Start with −1 ≤ sin 3x ≤ 1 for every x. Multiply all parts by 3: −3 ≤ 3 sin 3x ≤ 3, so the range is [−3, 3].

mcqs.q: The function tan (1)/(2) x is undefined at which values of x?
mcqs.why: tan t is undefined when t = (2n + 1)(π)/(2). Put t = (1)/(2) x: (1)/(2) x = (2n + 1)(π)/(2), multiply by 2 to get x = (2n + 1)π.

mcqs.q: What is the period of cosec 2x?
mcqs.why: The period of cosec t is 2π. With t = 2x, period = (2π)/(2) = π, by dividing the basic period by the coefficient 2.

mcqs.q: What is the period of cos 4x?
mcqs.why: The period of cos t is 2π. With t = 4x, period = (2π)/(4) = (π)/(2), after dividing by the coefficient 4.

mcqs.q: What is the range of 6 sec 2x?
mcqs.why: sec t satisfies sec t ≤ −1 or sec t ≥ 1. Multiply by 6: 6 sec 2x ≤ −6 or 6 sec 2x ≥ 6, so the range excludes (−6, 6).

mcqs.q: sec (π)/(4) x is undefined when x equals which form?
mcqs.why: sec t is undefined when t = (2n + 1)(π)/(2). Put t = (π)/(4) x and multiply by (4)/(π): x = 2(2n + 1) = 4n + 2.

mcqs.q: What is the maximum value of y = −2 + (1)/(2) sin((1)/(3) θ + 2)?
mcqs.why: For y = a + b sin(...), maximum = a + |b|. Here a = −2 and b = (1)/(2), so maximum = −2 + (1)/(2) = −(3)/(2).

mcqs.q: What are the maximum and minimum values of y = 5 − 4 sin(θ + 30)?
mcqs.why: Here a = 5 and b = −4, so |b| = 4. Maximum = a + |b| = 5 + 4 = 9; minimum = a − |b| = 5 − 4 = 1.

mcqs.q: What is the maximum value of y = (1)/(19 − 10 sin(3θ − 45))?
mcqs.why: Denominator: maximum = 19 + 10 = 29 and minimum = 19 − 10 = 9. A positive reciprocal is largest when the denominator is smallest, so maximum y = (1)/(9).

lessons.title: Exercise 12.2
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • y = 2 sin x on [0, 2π] has amplitude 2, period 2π, range [−2, 2], peak (π/2, 2) and trough (3π/2, −2).
  • y = cos 2x has period π, so two complete cycles fit in [0, 2π]; its x-intercepts there are π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4 and 7π/4.
  • y = −4 + sin x on [0, π] has range [−4, −3], centre line y = −4 and no intercepts.
  • y = −cot x has period π, asymptotes x = −π, 0, π on [−π, π], and value −1 at x = π/4.
  • y = 2 cosec 2x has period π, range y ≤ −2 or y ≥ 2, and a lowest point (π/4, 2) on its first branch.
  • y = sec (x)/(2) on π ≤ x ≤ 2π has range (−∞, −1], with value −2 at x = (4π)/(3) and −1 at x = 2π.
  • For y = sin Aθ or cos Aθ: period = (2π)/(A), frequency = (A)/(2π), amplitude = 1 for the unscaled functions in Q2.
  • Identities from symmetry: sin((π)/(2) + θ) = cos θ, cos((π)/(2) + θ) = −sin θ, sin(π − θ) = sin θ, cos(π − θ) = −cos θ, tan(π − θ) = −tan θ and tan(2π − θ) = −tan θ; also f(θ + 2kπ) = f(θ) for all six ratios, k ∈ Z.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Draw the graph of y = 2 sin x in the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π

Ans: Method: stretch the graph of y = sin x vertically by the factor 2.
Amplitude = 2.
Period = 2π.
Domain (as asked) = [0, 2π].
Range = [−2, 2].
Table of key values: x = 0, y = 0.
x = (π)/(6), y = 1.
x = (π)/(3), y = √3 ≈ 1.73.
x = (π)/(2), y = 2.
x = (2π)/(3), y = √3 ≈ 1.73.
x = (5π)/(6), y = 1.
x = π, y = 0.
x = (7π)/(6), y = −1.
x = (4π)/(3), y = −√3 ≈ −1.73.
x = (3π)/(2), y = −2.
x = (5π)/(3), y = −√3 ≈ −1.73.
x = (11π)/(6), y = −1.
x = 2π, y = 0.
Intercepts: (0, 0), (π, 0) and (2π, 0); the y-intercept is 0.
Asymptotes: none.
Graph (in words): a single sine wave of height 2 drawn from (0, 0); it rises smoothly to its peak (π/2, 2), falls back through (π, 0), continues down to its trough (3π/2, −2), and rises again to end at (2π, 0), exactly like y = sin x but with every height doubled.

Q: Q1(ii). Draw the graph of y = cos 2x in the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π

Ans: Method: compress the graph of y = cos x horizontally by the factor 2.
Amplitude = 1.
Period = (2π)/(2) = π, so two complete cycles fit in [0, 2π].
Domain (as asked) = [0, 2π].
Range = [−1, 1].
Table of key values over one period [0, π]: x = 0, y = 1.
x = (π)/(4), y = 0.
x = (π)/(2), y = −1.
x = (3π)/(4), y = 0.
x = π, y = 1.
The same values repeat on [π, 2π]: x = (5π)/(4), y = 0; x = (3π)/(2), y = −1; x = (7π)/(4), y = 0; x = 2π, y = 1.
Intercepts: y-intercept (0, 1); x-intercepts (π/4, 0), (3π/4, 0), (5π/4, 0), (7π/4, 0).
Asymptotes: none.
Graph (in words): a cosine wave squeezed to half its usual width; it starts at its peak (0, 1), falls through (π/4, 0) to a trough at (π/2, −1), returns to a peak at (π, 1), and then repeats the identical cycle once more between π and 2π.

Q: Q1(iii). Draw the graph of y = −4 + sin x in the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ π

Ans: Method: shift the graph of y = sin x down by 4 units.
Amplitude = 1, about the centre line y = −4.
Period = 2π; only the first half of a period is drawn.
Domain (as asked) = [0, π].
Range = [−4, −3].
Table of key values: x = 0, y = −4.
x = (π)/(6), y = −4 + (1)/(2) = −3.5.
x = (π)/(2), y = −4 + 1 = −3.
x = (5π)/(6), y = −3.5.
x = π, y = −4.
Intercepts: none; the whole graph lies below the x-axis.
Asymptotes: none.
Graph (in words): a shallow hump lying entirely between the lines y = −4 and y = −3; it starts at (0, −4), rises smoothly to its highest point (π/2, −3), and falls symmetrically back to (π, −4), like the top half of a sine wave pushed 4 units downward.

Q: Q1(iv). Draw the graph of y = −cot x in the interval −π ≤ x ≤ π

Ans: Method: reflect the graph of y = cot x in the x-axis.
Period = π.
Domain (as asked) = [−π, π] excluding x = −π, 0, π, where cot x is not defined.
Range = R.
Table of key values: x = −(3π)/(4), y = −1.
x = −(π)/(2), y = 0.
x = −(π)/(4), y = 1.
x = (π)/(4), y = −1.
x = (π)/(2), y = 0.
x = (3π)/(4), y = 1.
Intercepts: (−π/2, 0) and (π/2, 0); there is no y-intercept.
Asymptotes: the vertical lines x = −π, x = 0 and x = π.
Graph (in words): two increasing branches, the mirror image (top to bottom) of the cotangent graph; on (0, π) the branch climbs from −∞ just to the right of x = 0, passes through (π/4, −1) and (π/2, 0), and shoots up to +∞ as x approaches π from the left; the branch on (−π, 0) is the same shape shifted by one period, climbing from −∞ near x = −π through (−π/2, 0) to +∞ as x approaches 0 from the left.

Q: Q1(v). Draw the graph of y = 2 cosec 2x in the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π

Ans: Method: take the graph of y = cosec x, compress it horizontally by the factor 2 and stretch it vertically by the factor 2.
Period = (2π)/(2) = π.
Domain (as asked) = [0, 2π] excluding x = 0, (π)/(2), π, (3π)/(2), 2π, where cosec 2x is not defined.
Range: y ≤ −2 or y ≥ 2.
Table of key values: x = (π)/(4), y = 2 cosec (π)/(2) = 2.
x = (3π)/(4), y = 2 cosec (3π)/(2) = −2.
x = (5π)/(4), y = 2 cosec (5π)/(2) = 2.
x = (7π)/(4), y = 2 cosec (7π)/(2) = −2.
Intercepts: none; the graph never meets either axis inside the interval.
Asymptotes: the vertical lines x = 0, x = (π)/(2), x = π, x = (3π)/(2) and x = 2π.
Graph (in words): a chain of U-shaped and cap-shaped branches that never enters the strip −2 < y < 2; on (0, π/2) a U with its bottom at (π/4, 2) falls from +∞ and rises back to +∞; on (π/2, π) an upside-down U (a cap) with its top at (3π/4, −2) hangs below y = −2; the same pair of branches repeats on (π, 3π/2) and (3π/2, 2π).

Q: Q1(vi). Draw the graph of y = sec (x)/(2) in the interval π ≤ x ≤ 2π

Ans: Method: stretch the graph of y = sec x horizontally by the factor 2; only the part with (x)/(2) between (π)/(2) and π is drawn.
Period = (2π)/((1)/(2)) = 4π; the given interval shows only a quarter of one period.
Domain (as asked) = (π, 2π]; at x = π the function is not defined because (x)/(2) = (π)/(2).
Range = (−∞, −1].
Table of key values: as x approaches π from the right, y → −∞.
x = (4π)/(3), y = sec (2π)/(3) = −2.
x = (3π)/(2), y = sec (3π)/(4) = −√2 ≈ −1.41.
x = 2π, y = sec π = −1.
Intercepts: none.
Asymptotes: the vertical line x = π at the left end of the interval.
Graph (in words): a single rising branch below the x-axis; it comes up from −∞ just to the right of the asymptote x = π, climbs with decreasing steepness through (4π/3, −2) and (3π/2, −√2), and levels off at its highest point (2π, −1), never rising above y = −1.

Q: Q2(i). Without drawing, guess the graph of y = cos 2θ. Also find its period, frequency and amplitude.

Ans: Method: for y = cos Aθ, the period is (2π)/(A), the frequency is (A)/(2π) and the amplitude is 1.
Here A = 2, and 2 > 1.
So the graph of cos θ is compressed in the θ-direction.
There are 2 periods in an interval of length 2π.
Period = (2π)/(A) = (2π)/(2) = π.
Frequency = (A)/(2π) = (2)/(2π) = (1)/(π).
Amplitude = 1.
Graph (in words): a cosine wave of the usual height, starting at (0, 1), but squeezed so that one complete cycle (peak, trough, peak) fits into an interval of length π instead of 2π, with zeros at θ = π/4, 3π/4, … and troughs of −1 at θ = π/2, 3π/2, ….
Answer: Period = π, Frequency = (1)/(π), Amplitude = 1.

Q: Q2(ii). Without drawing, guess the graph of y = sin 6θ. Also find its period, frequency and amplitude.

Ans: Method: for y = sin Aθ, the period is (2π)/(A), the frequency is (A)/(2π) and the amplitude is 1.
Here A = 6, and 6 > 1.
So the graph of sin θ is strongly compressed in the θ-direction.
There are 6 periods in an interval of length 2π.
Period = (2π)/(A) = (2π)/(6) = (π)/(3).
Frequency = (A)/(2π) = (6)/(2π) = (3)/(π).
Amplitude = 1.
Graph (in words): a sine wave of the usual height 1, squeezed so that six complete waves fit between 0 and 2π; it crosses zero at every multiple of π/6, reaches 1 at θ = π/12, 5π/12, … and −1 at θ = π/4, 7π/12, ….
Answer: Period = (π)/(3), Frequency = (3)/(π), Amplitude = 1.

Q: Q2(iii). Without drawing, guess the graph of y = sin πθ. Also find its period, frequency and amplitude.

Ans: Method: for y = sin Aθ, the period is (2π)/(A), the frequency is (A)/(2π) and the amplitude is 1.
Here A = π ≈ 3.14, and A > 1.
So the graph of sin θ is compressed in the θ-direction.
There are π periods in an interval of length 2π.
Period = (2π)/(A) = (2π)/(π) = 2.
Frequency = (A)/(2π) = (π)/(2π) = (1)/(2).
Amplitude = 1.
Graph (in words): a sine wave of height 1 with a cycle of length 2; it starts at (0, 0), peaks at (1/2, 1), returns to zero at θ = 1, dips to (3/2, −1) and completes the cycle at θ = 2.
Answer: Period = 2, Frequency = (1)/(2), Amplitude = 1.

Q: Q2(iv). Without drawing, guess the graph of y = cos (π)/(2) θ. Also find its period, frequency and amplitude.

Ans: Method: for y = cos Aθ, the period is (2π)/(A), the frequency is (A)/(2π) and the amplitude is 1.
Here A = (π)/(2) ≈ 1.57, and A > 1.
So the graph of cos θ is slightly compressed in the θ-direction.
There are (π)/(2) periods in an interval of length 2π.
Period = (2π)/(A) = (2π)/((π)/(2)) = 4.
Frequency = (A)/(2π) = ((π)/(2))/(2π) = (1)/(4).
Amplitude = 1.
Graph (in words): a cosine wave of height 1 with a cycle of length 4; it starts at (0, 1), crosses zero at θ = 1, bottoms at (2, −1), crosses zero again at θ = 3 and returns to (4, 1).
Answer: Period = 4, Frequency = (1)/(4), Amplitude = 1.

Q: Q3(i). Use the symmetric and periodic properties of the sine, cosine and tangent functions to establish the identity: sin((π)/(2) + θ) = cos θ

Ans: Method: use sin((π)/(2) − φ) = cos φ with φ = −θ, then the even property of cosine.
Put φ = −θ in sin((π)/(2) − φ) = cos φ.
Then (π)/(2) + θ = (π)/(2) − (−θ), so sin((π)/(2) + θ) = cos(−θ).
Cosine is an even function: cos(−θ) = cos θ.
Therefore sin((π)/(2) + θ) = cos θ.
Hence proved.

Q: Q3(ii). Use the symmetric and periodic properties of the sine, cosine and tangent functions to establish the identity: cos((π)/(2) + θ) = −sin θ

Ans: Method: use cos((π)/(2) − φ) = sin φ with φ = −θ, then the odd property of sine.
Put φ = −θ in cos((π)/(2) − φ) = sin φ.
Then (π)/(2) + θ = (π)/(2) − (−θ), so cos((π)/(2) + θ) = sin(−θ).
Sine is an odd function: sin(−θ) = −sin θ.
Therefore cos((π)/(2) + θ) = −sin θ.
Hence proved.

Q: Q3(iii). Use the symmetric and periodic properties of the sine, cosine and tangent functions to establish the identity: sin(π − θ) = sin θ

Ans: Method: use the odd property of sine and its translation property sin(θ − π) = −sin θ.
π − θ = −(θ − π).
So sin(π − θ) = sin(−(θ − π)).
By the odd property, sin(−(θ − π)) = −sin(θ − π).
By the translation property, sin(θ − π) = −sin θ.
So sin(π − θ) = −(−sin θ) = sin θ.
Hence proved.

Q: Q3(iv). Use the symmetric and periodic properties of the sine, cosine and tangent functions to establish the identity: cos(π − θ) = −cos θ

Ans: Method: use the even property of cosine and its translation property cos(θ − π) = −cos θ.
π − θ = −(θ − π).
So cos(π − θ) = cos(−(θ − π)).
By the even property, cos(−(θ − π)) = cos(θ − π).
By the translation property, cos(θ − π) = −cos θ.
So cos(π − θ) = −cos θ.
Hence proved.

Q: Q3(v). Use the symmetric and periodic properties of the sine, cosine and tangent functions to establish the identity: tan(π − θ) = −tan θ

Ans: Method: write tan as (sin)/(cos) and use the results of parts (iii) and (iv).
tan(π − θ) = (sin(π − θ))/(cos(π − θ)).
By part (iii), sin(π − θ) = sin θ.
By part (iv), cos(π − θ) = −cos θ.
So tan(π − θ) = (sin θ)/(−cos θ) = −tan θ.
Hence proved.

Q: Q3(vi). Use the symmetric and periodic properties of the sine, cosine and tangent functions to establish the identity: tan(2π − θ) = −tan θ

Ans: Method: use the periodic property of tangent (period π) and then its odd property.
2π is a multiple of the period π of tan θ.
So tan(2π − θ) = tan(−θ + 2π) = tan(−θ).
By the odd property, tan(−θ) = −tan θ.
So tan(2π − θ) = −tan θ.
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(i). For any integer k, deduce that sin(θ + 2kπ) = sin θ

Ans: Method: apply the periodic property sin(θ + 2π) = sin θ repeatedly.
For k = 1: sin(θ + 2π) = sin θ, by the periodic property.
Suppose sin(θ + 2kπ) = sin θ for some positive integer k.
Then sin(θ + 2(k + 1)π) = sin((θ + 2kπ) + 2π).
= sin(θ + 2kπ), by the periodic property applied to the angle θ + 2kπ.
= sin θ, by the supposition.
So the result holds for every positive integer k, and also for k = 0.
For negative k, use sin(θ − 2π) = sin θ repeatedly in the same way.
Therefore sin(θ + 2kπ) = sin θ for every integer k.
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(ii). For any integer k, deduce that cos(θ + 2kπ) = cos θ

Ans: Method: apply the periodic property cos(θ + 2π) = cos θ repeatedly.
For k = 1: cos(θ + 2π) = cos θ, by the periodic property.
Suppose cos(θ + 2kπ) = cos θ for some positive integer k.
Then cos(θ + 2(k + 1)π) = cos((θ + 2kπ) + 2π).
= cos(θ + 2kπ), by the periodic property applied to the angle θ + 2kπ.
= cos θ, by the supposition.
So the result holds for every positive integer k, and also for k = 0.
For negative k, use cos(θ − 2π) = cos θ repeatedly in the same way.
Therefore cos(θ + 2kπ) = cos θ for every integer k.
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(iii). For any integer k, deduce that tan(θ + 2kπ) = tan θ

Ans: Method: apply the periodic property of tangent, whose period is π; 2kπ is a multiple of π.
The period of tan θ is π, so tan(θ + π) = tan θ.
Adding π a total of 2k times gives tan(θ + 2kπ) = tan θ for every positive integer k.
The same repetition with tan(θ − π) = tan θ gives the result for negative k, and k = 0 is trivial.
Therefore tan(θ + 2kπ) = tan θ for every integer k.
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(iv). For any integer k, deduce that cot(θ + 2kπ) = cot θ

Ans: Method: apply the periodic property of cotangent, whose period is π; 2kπ is a multiple of π.
The period of cot θ is π, so cot(θ + π) = cot θ.
Adding π a total of 2k times gives cot(θ + 2kπ) = cot θ for every positive integer k.
The same repetition with cot(θ − π) = cot θ gives the result for negative k, and k = 0 is trivial.
Therefore cot(θ + 2kπ) = cot θ for every integer k.
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(v). For any integer k, deduce that sec(θ + 2kπ) = sec θ

Ans: Method: sec is the reciprocal of cos, whose period is 2π.
By part (ii), cos(θ + 2kπ) = cos θ for every integer k.
Take reciprocals of both sides.
(1)/(cos(θ + 2kπ)) = (1)/(cos θ).
That is, sec(θ + 2kπ) = sec θ, wherever both sides are defined.
Therefore sec(θ + 2kπ) = sec θ for every integer k.
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(vi). For any integer k, deduce that cosec(θ + 2kπ) = cosec θ

Ans: Method: cosec is the reciprocal of sin, whose period is 2π.
By part (i), sin(θ + 2kπ) = sin θ for every integer k.
Take reciprocals of both sides.
(1)/(sin(θ + 2kπ)) = (1)/(sin θ).
That is, cosec(θ + 2kπ) = cosec θ, wherever both sides are defined.
Therefore cosec(θ + 2kπ) = cosec θ for every integer k.
Hence proved.

mcqs.q: For y = 2 sin x on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π, what is the amplitude?
mcqs.why: Amplitude is the vertical stretch factor multiplying sin x. In y = 2 sin x that factor is 2, so the graph reaches y = 2 and y = −2.

mcqs.q: At x = (π)/(2), what is the value of y = 2 sin x?
mcqs.why: Substitute x = (π)/(2): y = 2 sin (π)/(2) = 2 × 1 = 2, which is the peak point (π/2, 2) in the table of key values.

mcqs.q: What is the period of y = cos 2x?
mcqs.why: Period of cos(bx) = (2π)/(b). Here b = 2, so period = (2π)/(2) = π; hence two cycles fit into [0, 2π].

mcqs.q: How many complete cycles of y = cos 2x fit in 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π?
mcqs.why: The interval length is 2π and one cycle has length π. Number of cycles = (2π)/(π) = 2, matching the repeated table on [0, π] and [π, 2π].

mcqs.q: What is the range of y = −4 + sin x on 0 ≤ x ≤ π?
mcqs.why: On [0, π], sin x goes from 0 up to 1 and back to 0. Subtract 4: the values go from −4 up to −4 + 1 = −3, so the range is [−4, −3].

mcqs.q: Which statement about the intercepts of y = −4 + sin x on 0 ≤ x ≤ π is correct?
options: It has no intercepts; the graph lies below the x-axis
mcqs.why: The range is [−4, −3], so y is never 0 and the graph never meets the x-axis. It starts at (0, −4), below the axis, so there are no intercepts in the interval.

mcqs.q: What is the period of y = −cot x?
mcqs.why: cot x has period π, and reflecting in the x-axis (the minus sign) does not change the period. So y = −cot x also has period π.

mcqs.q: What is the value of y = −cot x at x = (π)/(4)?
mcqs.why: cot (π)/(4) = 1, so −cot (π)/(4) = −1. This is the table value used for the branch on (0, π).

mcqs.q: What is the range of y = 2 cosec 2x?
mcqs.why: cosec t satisfies cosec t ≤ −1 or cosec t ≥ 1. Multiply by 2: 2 cosec 2x ≤ −2 or 2 cosec 2x ≥ 2, so the strip −2 < y < 2 is never entered.

mcqs.q: Which line is a vertical asymptote of y = 2 cosec 2x on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π?
mcqs.why: cosec 2x is undefined when 2x = nπ, i.e. x = (nπ)/(2): x = 0, π/2, π, 3π/2, 2π. Of the options only x = (π)/(2) is in that list.

mcqs.q: What is the range of y = sec (x)/(2) on π ≤ x ≤ 2π?
mcqs.why: On this interval (x)/(2) runs from (π)/(2) to π, where sec goes from −∞ up to sec π = −1. So the values are y ≤ −1, i.e. the range (−∞, −1].

mcqs.q: For y = cos 2θ, what is the frequency?
mcqs.why: Frequency = (A)/(2π) for y = cos Aθ. Here A = 2, so frequency = (2)/(2π) = (1)/(π), with period (2π)/(2) = π and amplitude 1.

mcqs.q: What is the period of y = sin 6θ?
mcqs.why: Period of sin Aθ = (2π)/(A). Here A = 6, so period = (2π)/(6) = (π)/(3); six periods fit in an interval of length 2π.

mcqs.q: For y = sin πθ, what is the frequency?
mcqs.why: Frequency = (A)/(2π) with A = π: frequency = (π)/(2π) = (1)/(2). The period is (2π)/(π) = 2 and the amplitude is 1.

mcqs.q: What is the period of y = cos (π)/(2) θ?
mcqs.why: Period = (2π)/(A) with A = (π)/(2): period = (2π)/((π)/(2)) = 2π × (2)/(π) = 4. The wave starts at (0, 1) and returns to (4, 1).

lessons.title: Exercise 12.3
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Graphically, sin θ = (√2)/(2) meets y = sin θ at θ = (π)/(4) and (3π)/(4) in [0, 2π); general solutions add 2nπ to each.
  • cos θ = −(√3)/(2) has solutions (5π)/(6) and (7π)/(6) in [0, 2π), with reference angle (π)/(6).
  • tan θ = √3 has the single solution (π)/(3) in one period; general solution θ = (π)/(3) + nπ.
  • cos θ = (1)/(2) has solutions (π)/(3) and (5π)/(3) in [0, 2π) — the second family is part of the correct answer.
  • tan θ = −1 gives θ = (3π)/(4) + nπ, using reference angle (π)/(4) and period π.
  • sin θ = −(1)/(2) has solutions (7π)/(6) and (11π)/(6) in [0, 2π), in quadrants III and IV.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Find all solutions of sin θ = (√2)/(2) graphically

Ans: Method: graph y = sin θ and the line y = (√2)/(2); the θ-coordinates of the intersection points are the solutions, then use the period 2π.
In 0 ≤ θ < 2π the curve y = sin θ meets the line y = (√2)/(2) at two points.
They are θ = (π)/(4) and θ = π − (π)/(4) = (3π)/(4).
Sine has period 2π, so add integer multiples of 2π to each solution.
θ = (π)/(4) + 2nπ, n ∈ Z.
or θ = (3π)/(4) + 2nπ, n ∈ Z.
Solution set: {(π)/(4) + 2nπ} ∪ {(3π)/(4) + 2nπ}, n is any integer.

Q: Q1(ii). Find all solutions of cos θ = −(√3)/(2) graphically

Ans: Method: graph y = cos θ and the line y = −(√3)/(2); read off the intersections, then use the period 2π.
cos (π)/(6) = (√3)/(2), so the reference angle is (π)/(6).
Cosine is negative in quadrants II and III.
In 0 ≤ θ < 2π the intersections are at θ = π − (π)/(6) = (5π)/(6) and θ = π + (π)/(6) = (7π)/(6).
Cosine has period 2π, so add integer multiples of 2π.
θ = (5π)/(6) + 2nπ, n ∈ Z.
or θ = (7π)/(6) + 2nπ, n ∈ Z.
Solution set: {(5π)/(6) + 2nπ} ∪ {(7π)/(6) + 2nπ}, n is any integer.

Q: Q1(iii). Find all solutions of tan θ = √3 graphically

Ans: Method: graph y = tan θ and the line y = √3; read off the intersection in one period, then use the period π.
tan (π)/(3) = √3.
In 0 ≤ θ < π the only intersection is at θ = (π)/(3).
Tangent has period π, so add integer multiples of π.
θ = (π)/(3) + nπ, n ∈ Z.
Solution set: {(π)/(3) + nπ}, n is any integer.

Q: Q1(iv). Find all solutions of cos θ = (1)/(2) graphically

Ans: Method: graph y = cos θ and the line y = (1)/(2); read off the intersections, then use the period 2π.
cos (π)/(3) = (1)/(2), so the reference angle is (π)/(3).
Cosine is positive in quadrants I and IV.
In 0 ≤ θ < 2π the intersections are at θ = (π)/(3) and θ = 2π − (π)/(3) = (5π)/(3).
Cosine has period 2π, so add integer multiples of 2π.
θ = (π)/(3) + 2nπ, n ∈ Z.
or θ = (5π)/(3) + 2nπ, n ∈ Z.
Solution set: {(π)/(3) + 2nπ} ∪ {(5π)/(3) + 2nπ}, n is any integer.
Note: The book's printed answer (θ = (π)/(3) + 2nπ only) is incorrect; the correct answer also includes θ = (5π)/(3) + 2nπ.

Q: Q1(v). Find all solutions of tan θ = −1 graphically

Ans: Method: graph y = tan θ and the line y = −1; read off the intersection in one period, then use the period π.
tan (π)/(4) = 1, so the reference angle is (π)/(4).
Tangent is negative in quadrants II and IV; in 0 ≤ θ < π the intersection is in quadrant II.
θ = π − (π)/(4) = (3π)/(4).
Tangent has period π, so add integer multiples of π.
θ = (3π)/(4) + nπ, n ∈ Z.
Solution set: {(3π)/(4) + nπ}, n is any integer.

Q: Q1(vi). Find all solutions of sin θ = −(1)/(2) graphically

Ans: Method: graph y = sin θ and the line y = −(1)/(2); read off the intersections, then use the period 2π.
sin (π)/(6) = (1)/(2), so the reference angle is (π)/(6).
Sine is negative in quadrants III and IV.
In 0 ≤ θ < 2π the intersections are at θ = π + (π)/(6) = (7π)/(6) and θ = 2π − (π)/(6) = (11π)/(6).
Sine has period 2π, so add integer multiples of 2π.
θ = (7π)/(6) + 2nπ, n ∈ Z.
or θ = (11π)/(6) + 2nπ, n ∈ Z.
Solution set: {(7π)/(6) + 2nπ} ∪ {(11π)/(6) + 2nπ}, n is any integer.

mcqs.q: In 0 ≤ θ < 2π, the graphical solutions of sin θ = (√2)/(2) are:
mcqs.why: The line y = (√2)/(2) cuts y = sin θ twice in [0, 2π): at θ = (π)/(4), and by symmetry at π − (π)/(4) = (3π)/(4).

mcqs.q: The general solution of sin θ = (√2)/(2) is:
mcqs.why: In one period the solutions are (π)/(4) and (3π)/(4). Sine has period 2π, so add 2nπ to each: θ = (π)/(4) + 2nπ or θ = (3π)/(4) + 2nπ.

mcqs.q: In 0 ≤ θ < 2π, the graphical solutions of cos θ = −(√3)/(2) are:
mcqs.why: Reference angle: cos (π)/(6) = (√3)/(2). Cosine is negative in quadrants II and III, giving π − (π)/(6) = (5π)/(6) and π + (π)/(6) = (7π)/(6).

mcqs.q: The general solution of tan θ = √3 is:
mcqs.why: tan (π)/(3) = √3, so in [0, π) the only intersection is θ = (π)/(3). Tangent has period π, so add nπ: θ = (π)/(3) + nπ.

mcqs.q: Which family must be included in the general solution of cos θ = (1)/(2), in addition to θ = (π)/(3) + 2nπ?
mcqs.why: cos (π)/(3) = (1)/(2) and cosine is positive in quadrants I and IV, so in [0, 2π) there is also θ = 2π − (π)/(3) = (5π)/(3). Add 2nπ to both families.

mcqs.q: The general solution of tan θ = −1 is:
mcqs.why: Reference angle (π)/(4) since tan (π)/(4) = 1. In [0, π) tangent is negative in quadrant II: θ = π − (π)/(4) = (3π)/(4). Period π gives θ = (3π)/(4) + nπ.

mcqs.q: In 0 ≤ θ < 2π, the graphical solutions of sin θ = −(1)/(2) are:
mcqs.why: Reference angle (π)/(6) since sin (π)/(6) = (1)/(2). Sine is negative in quadrants III and IV: π + (π)/(6) = (7π)/(6) and 2π − (π)/(6) = (11π)/(6).

mcqs.q: When solving tan θ = k graphically, multiples of which period are added to the solution in one period?
mcqs.why: The graph of y = tan θ repeats every π, so each intersection repeats after adding nπ. That is why tan θ = √3 gives θ = (π)/(3) + nπ, not + 2nπ.

mcqs.q: For cos θ = −(√3)/(2), the reference angle used in the graphical solution is:
mcqs.why: Take the positive value: cos α = (√3)/(2) gives α = (π)/(6), because cos (π)/(6) = (√3)/(2). The actual solutions are then π − α and π + α.

mcqs.q: The solution set of sin θ = (√2)/(2), written as a union, is:
mcqs.why: Two intersections per period, at (π)/(4) and (3π)/(4), each repeated with period 2π. Combining both families gives the stated union over all integers n.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.4
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • arc sin(−1) (general relation) = {−(π)/(2) + 2nπ, n ∈ Z}.
  • arc cos(−(√2)/(2)) = {(3π)/(4) + 2nπ} ∪ {(5π)/(4) + 2nπ}, n ∈ Z.
  • arc tan(−(√3)/(3)) = {−(π)/(6) + nπ, n ∈ Z}, using the period π of tangent.
  • Principal ranges: Arc cos [0, π], Sin⁻¹ [−(π)/(2), (π)/(2)], Tan⁻¹ (−(π)/(2), (π)/(2)).
  • Arc cos[tan (3π)/(4)] = π (principal value), since tan (3π)/(4) = −1.
  • Sin[Tan⁻¹((1)/(√3))] = (1)/(2) and Sin[Arc cos(−(√3)/(2))] = (1)/(2) using principal values.
  • tan[Arc cos(−(4)/(5))] = −(3)/(4), from sin y = (3)/(5) when cos y = −(4)/(5) in quadrant II.
  • Cos[Sin⁻¹((√2)/(2))] = (√2)/(2), Sec[Cos⁻¹((1)/(2))] = 2, Cosec[Tan⁻¹(1)] = √2, Sec[Sin⁻¹((1)/(2))] = (2√3)/(3); a function and its inverse cancel, e.g. tan(Tan⁻¹ u) = u.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Evaluate the inverse relation of the general trigonometric function: arc sin(−1)

Ans: Method: y = arc sin(−1) means sin y = −1, with y any real number (general relation, no principal restriction).
We need every angle whose sine is −1.
In [0, 2π) the only such angle is y = (3π)/(2), which is the same direction as −(π)/(2).
Sine has period 2π, so add integer multiples of 2π.
y = −(π)/(2) + 2nπ, n ∈ Z.
Answer: {−(π)/(2) + 2nπ, n ∈ Z}.

Q: Q1(ii). Evaluate the inverse relation of the general trigonometric function: arc cos(−(√2)/(2))

Ans: Method: y = arc cos(−(√2)/(2)) means cos y = −(√2)/(2) = −(1)/(√2), with y any real number.
cos (π)/(4) = (1)/(√2), so the reference angle is (π)/(4).
Cosine is negative in quadrants II and III.
In [0, 2π) the angles are y = π − (π)/(4) = (3π)/(4) and y = π + (π)/(4) = (5π)/(4).
Cosine has period 2π, so add integer multiples of 2π.
y = (3π)/(4) + 2nπ or y = (5π)/(4) + 2nπ, n ∈ Z.
Answer: {(3π)/(4) + 2nπ, n ∈ Z} ∪ {(5π)/(4) + 2nπ, n ∈ Z}.

Q: Q1(iii). Evaluate the inverse relation of the general trigonometric function: arc tan(−(√3)/(3))

Ans: Method: y = arc tan(−(√3)/(3)) means tan y = −(√3)/(3) = −(1)/(√3), with y any real number.
tan (π)/(6) = (1)/(√3), so the reference angle is (π)/(6).
Tangent is negative in quadrants II and IV; in one period the value is y = −(π)/(6).
Tangent has period π, so add integer multiples of π.
y = −(π)/(6) + nπ, n ∈ Z.
Answer: {−(π)/(6) + nπ, n ∈ Z}.

Q: Q2(i). Compute Arc cos[tan (3π)/(4)]

Ans: Method: evaluate the inner function first, then use the principal-value range of Arc cos, which is [0, π].
tan (3π)/(4) = −1.
So we need Arc cos(−1).
Let y = Arc cos(−1); then cos y = −1 with 0 ≤ y ≤ π.
The angle in [0, π] with cosine −1 is y = π.
The general values of cos⁻¹(−1) are π + 2nπ, n ∈ Z, as listed in the book's answer key.
Answer: π + 2nπ, n ∈ Z (principal value π).

Q: Q2(ii). Compute Sin[Tan⁻¹((1)/(√3))]

Ans: Method: evaluate the principal inverse function first; Tan⁻¹ has range (−(π)/(2), (π)/(2)).
Let y = Tan⁻¹((1)/(√3)); then Tan y = (1)/(√3) with −(π)/(2) < y < (π)/(2).
The angle there with tangent (1)/(√3) is y = (π)/(6).
Now Sin[Tan⁻¹((1)/(√3))] = Sin((π)/(6)).
= (1)/(2).
Answer: (1)/(2).

Q: Q2(iii). Compute Sin[Arc cos(−(√3)/(2))]

Ans: Method: evaluate the principal inverse function first; Arc cos has range [0, π].
Let y = Arc cos(−(√3)/(2)); then cos y = −(√3)/(2) with 0 ≤ y ≤ π.
cos (π)/(6) = (√3)/(2), and cosine is negative in quadrant II.
So y = π − (π)/(6) = (5π)/(6).
Now Sin[Arc cos(−(√3)/(2))] = Sin((5π)/(6)).
= (1)/(2).
Answer: (1)/(2).
Note: The book's printed answer {−(1)/(2), (1)/(2)} also includes the value obtained from the general (non-principal) values of cos⁻¹(−(√3)/(2)); the principal value is (1)/(2).

Q: Q2(iv). Compute tan[Arc cos(−(4)/(5))]

Ans: Method: let y = Arc cos(−(4)/(5)), work out sin y from cos y, then form tan y; Arc cos has range [0, π].
Let y = Arc cos(−(4)/(5)); then cos y = −(4)/(5) with 0 ≤ y ≤ π.
So y is in quadrant II, where sine is positive.
sin y = √(1 − cos²y) = √(1 − (16)/(25)) = √((9)/(25)) = (3)/(5).
tan y = (sin y)/(cos y) = ((3)/(5))/(−(4)/(5)) = −(3)/(4).
Answer: −(3)/(4).

Q: Q3(i). Find the exact value of Cos[Sin⁻¹ (√2)/(2)]

Ans: Method: principal-value ranges: Sin⁻¹ has range [−(π)/(2), (π)/(2)] and Cos is the principal cosine function.
Let y = Sin⁻¹((√2)/(2)); then Sin y = (√2)/(2) with −(π)/(2) ≤ y ≤ (π)/(2).
The angle there with sine (√2)/(2) is y = (π)/(4).
Cos[Sin⁻¹((√2)/(2))] = Cos((π)/(4)).
= (√2)/(2).
Answer: (√2)/(2).

Q: Q3(ii). Find the exact value of Tan[Cos⁻¹ (√3)/(2)]

Ans: Method: principal-value ranges: Cos⁻¹ has range [0, π] and Tan is the principal tangent function.
Let y = Cos⁻¹((√3)/(2)); then Cos y = (√3)/(2) with 0 ≤ y ≤ π.
The angle there with cosine (√3)/(2) is y = (π)/(6), which lies in the domain of principal Tan.
Tan[Cos⁻¹((√3)/(2))] = Tan((π)/(6)).
= (1)/(√3) = (√3)/(3).
Answer: (√3)/(3).

Q: Q3(iii). Find the exact value of Sec[Cos⁻¹ (1)/(2)]

Ans: Method: principal-value range: Cos⁻¹ has range [0, π].
Let y = Cos⁻¹((1)/(2)); then Cos y = (1)/(2) with 0 ≤ y ≤ π.
The angle there with cosine (1)/(2) is y = (π)/(3).
Sec[Cos⁻¹((1)/(2))] = Sec((π)/(3)) = (1)/(Cos (π)/(3)).
= (1)/((1)/(2)) = 2.
Answer: 2.

Q: Q3(iv). Find the exact value of Cosec[Tan⁻¹(1)]

Ans: Method: principal-value range: Tan⁻¹ has range (−(π)/(2), (π)/(2)).
Let y = Tan⁻¹(1); then Tan y = 1 with −(π)/(2) < y < (π)/(2).
The angle there with tangent 1 is y = (π)/(4).
Cosec[Tan⁻¹(1)] = cosec (π)/(4) = (1)/(sin (π)/(4)).
= (1)/((√2)/(2)) = √2.
Answer: √2.

Q: Q3(v). Find the exact value of Sin[Tan⁻¹(−1)]

Ans: Method: principal-value ranges: Tan⁻¹ has range (−(π)/(2), (π)/(2)) and Sin is the principal sine function.
Let y = Tan⁻¹(−1); then Tan y = −1 with −(π)/(2) < y < (π)/(2).
The angle there with tangent −1 is y = −(π)/(4).
Sin[Tan⁻¹(−1)] = Sin(−(π)/(4)).
= −(√2)/(2).
Answer: −(√2)/(2).

Q: Q3(vi). Find the exact value of Sec[Sin⁻¹((1)/(2))]

Ans: Method: principal-value range: Sin⁻¹ has range [−(π)/(2), (π)/(2)].
Let y = Sin⁻¹((1)/(2)); then Sin y = (1)/(2) with −(π)/(2) ≤ y ≤ (π)/(2).
The angle there with sine (1)/(2) is y = (π)/(6).
Sec[Sin⁻¹((1)/(2))] = Sec((π)/(6)) = (1)/(cos (π)/(6)).
= (1)/((√3)/(2)) = (2)/(√3) = (2√3)/(3).
Answer: (2√3)/(3).

Q: Q4(i). Simplify cosec(Sin⁻¹ (1)/(u)), taking u as a positive number

Ans: Method: let y = Sin⁻¹((1)/(u)) and use Sin y = (1)/(u); this needs u ≥ 1 for Sin⁻¹ to be defined.
Let y = Sin⁻¹((1)/(u)), so Sin y = (1)/(u), with y in [−(π)/(2), (π)/(2)].
cosec y = (1)/(Sin y).
= (1)/((1)/(u)).
= u.
So cosec(Sin⁻¹((1)/(u))) = u.
Answer: u.

Q: Q4(ii). Simplify tan(Tan⁻¹ u), taking u as a positive number

Ans: Method: a function and its inverse cancel: tan(Tan⁻¹ u) = u for every real u.
Let y = Tan⁻¹ u, so Tan y = u with −(π)/(2) < y < (π)/(2).
The (general) tangent of this same angle y is also u.
So tan(Tan⁻¹ u) = u.
Answer: u.

Q: Q4(iii). Simplify tan(Cos⁻¹ (1)/(√(1 + u²))), taking u as a positive number

Ans: Method: let y = Cos⁻¹((1)/(√(1 + u²))), find sin y from cos y, then form tan y; Cos⁻¹ has range [0, π].
Let y = Cos⁻¹((1)/(√(1 + u²))); then Cos y = (1)/(√(1 + u²)) with 0 ≤ y ≤ π.
Since u > 0, Cos y > 0, so y is in quadrant I and sin y is positive.
sin y = √(1 − Cos²y) = √(1 − (1)/(1 + u²)) = √((u²)/(1 + u²)) = (u)/(√(1 + u²)).
tan y = (sin y)/(Cos y) = ((u)/(√(1 + u²)))/((1)/(√(1 + u²))) = u.
Answer: u.

Q: Q4(iv). Simplify Cos⁻¹(cos √(1 − u²)), taking u as a positive number

Ans: Method: Cos⁻¹(cos θ) = θ whenever θ lies in the principal range [0, π] of Cos⁻¹.
Let θ = √(1 − u²).
For 0 < u ≤ 1, 0 ≤ θ < 1, and 1 < π, so θ ∈ [0, π].
Therefore Cos⁻¹(cos θ) = θ.
That is, Cos⁻¹(cos √(1 − u²)) = √(1 − u²).
Answer: √(1 − u²).

mcqs.q: The general inverse relation arc sin(−1) equals:
mcqs.why: Solve sin y = −1 with no principal restriction. In [0, 2π) the only angle is (3π)/(2) = −(π)/(2) in direction; add the period 2π: y = −(π)/(2) + 2nπ.

mcqs.q: The general inverse relation arc cos(−(√2)/(2)) equals:
mcqs.why: cos (π)/(4) = (√2)/(2), reference angle (π)/(4). Cosine is negative in quadrants II and III: π − (π)/(4) = (3π)/(4) and π + (π)/(4) = (5π)/(4); add 2nπ to each.

mcqs.q: The general inverse relation arc tan(−(√3)/(3)) equals:
mcqs.why: tan (π)/(6) = (1)/(√3) = (√3)/(3), so the value in one period is y = −(π)/(6). Tangent has period π, so add nπ: y = −(π)/(6) + nπ.

mcqs.q: The principal value of Arc cos[tan (3π)/(4)] is:
mcqs.why: First tan (3π)/(4) = −1. Then Arc cos(−1) is the angle y in [0, π] with cos y = −1, which is y = π. So the principal value is π.

mcqs.q: Sin[Tan⁻¹((1)/(√3))] equals:
Using the principal value, Sin[Arc cos(−(√3)/(2))] equals:
mcqs.why: Let y = Arc cos(−(√3)/(2)): cos y = −(√3)/(2) with 0 ≤ y ≤ π, so y = π − (π)/(6) = (5π)/(6). Then Sin y = Sin (5π)/(6) = (1)/(2). The book also lists −(1)/(2), which comes from non-principal values and is not the principal value.

mcqs.q: tan[Arc cos(−(4)/(5))] equals:
mcqs.why: Let y = Arc cos(−(4)/(5)): cos y = −(4)/(5), 0 ≤ y ≤ π, so y is in quadrant II and sin y is positive. sin y = √(1 − (16)/(25)) = (3)/(5). tan y = ((3)/(5))/(−(4)/(5)) = −(3)/(4).
